sections.title: Article 90 — Introduction: how this Code is set up
sections.plain_explanation:
Article 90 is the front door of the Code. Before any wiring rule, it answers four questions: why the Code exists, what it covers, how the book is arranged, and who enforces it.
• 90.1, purpose: practical safeguarding of people and property from the hazards of using electricity. Followed with proper maintenance, the Code gives an installation essentially free from hazard — but it is a safety floor, not a design manual, and it does not promise the most efficient or convenient system.
• 90.2, scope: the Code covers premises wiring in buildings, yards, parking areas and similar locations. It does not cover most utility-owned generation and distribution, ships, railway rolling stock or mining equipment.
• 90.3, arrangement: Chapters 1 through 4 apply generally. Chapters 5, 6 and 7 cover special places, equipment and conditions, and they supplement or modify the general chapters. Chapter 8 stands apart — the general chapters reach it only where a Chapter 8 rule points back. Chapter 9 holds the tables, and the annexes explain; they do not require.
• 90.4, enforcement: the authority having jurisdiction (AHJ) enforces the Code and approves equipment and installations, and can grant special permission where the Code allows it.
• 90.5, how rules are written: 'shall' is mandatory, 'shall be permitted' allows an option, and Informational Notes only explain — a note by itself is not a requirement.
sections.on_the_job: Start here when the question is really about whether the Code applies at all, who enforces it, or whether a note in the book is a requirement. On a Florida job the permit date picks the edition: a permit applied for in November 2026 is inspected to NEC 2020 under the FBC 8th Edition (see the Florida note below). And when a handbook, a brochure or this app reads a rule one way and the inspector reads it another, the AHJ's reading is the one your job is judged by (90.4).

NEC 2023 takes effect in Florida with the FBC 9th Edition for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026.
sections.why_it_exists: Most code arguments are really Article 90 arguments: does this book even apply here, who gets to decide, and can a note fail you? Article 90 settles those questions before they turn into a fight at the inspection.
inspection_fails: Arguing an Informational Note as a requirement — or waving off a 'shall' rule because a note seemed to soften it (90.5).
Designing the utility side of a service to the NEC — utility-owned generation and distribution sit outside the coverage in 90.2.
Installing equipment the AHJ has not approved, or doing work that needs special permission without the AHJ's written grant (90.4).
Applying the general chapters straight into a Chapter 8 communications job — Chapter 8 stands apart unless its own rule points back (90.3).
sections.exam_trap: The trap answer quotes an Informational Note as if it were a rule. Notes explain and point to other material; they cannot create a requirement, and they cannot override a 'shall' (90.5). The other trap: calling the Code a design manual. It is a safety floor (90.1).

sections.title: Purpose of the Code
sections.plain_explanation:
90.1 states the Code's one job: the practical safeguarding of persons and property from hazards arising from the use of electricity.
• Compliance with the Code, together with proper maintenance, results in an installation that is essentially free from hazard.
• It does not promise the most efficient or most convenient system. The Code sets the safety floor; efficiency, convenience and good design are built above it.
• The Code is not a design manual, and it is not an instruction manual for untrained persons. It states the minimum an installation must meet, not the best installation that can be built.
sections.on_the_job: When a plan meets the Code but works poorly, that is a design problem, not proof the Code failed. When a shortcut works but is hazardous, the Code still controls. Build to the safety floor first, then to good design above it. On a Sharma rough-in, that means the floor is not negotiable: if a builder asks to drop a required GFCI or a required circuit to save money, the answer is no — 90.1 is the reason. Upgrades above the floor, like extra receptacles or a larger service, are the customer's choice; the floor is not.

sections.why_it_exists: Every rule in the book traces back to this sentence. Electricity is useful precisely because it carries energy, and that energy starts fires and kills quietly when it escapes its path. The purpose clause is also the tie-breaker: when two readings of a rule are possible, the reading that protects people and property is the one the Code intends.
inspection_fails: Work installed from a video or a handbook instead of the adopted Code, red-tagged where it conflicts with the NEC.
'It works fine' offered as the defense for a missing required protection — operation is not compliance, and the correction notice stands.
A required protection value-engineered out at the customer's request; the AHJ cites the rule, not the customer's preference.
A design choice enforced as if it were a Code rule — or a Code rule waived as 'just design.' The floor and the design above it are different things.
sections.exam_trap: The trap answer says the Code is a design manual that guarantees an efficient, convenient installation. 90.1 says the opposite: it is a safety standard. Compliance gives an installation essentially free from hazard — not necessarily efficient or convenient — and the Code is not a design manual or an instruction book for untrained persons.

sections.title: Scope — what is covered and what is not
sections.plain_explanation: This section lists the kinds of installations the Code covers, such as premises wiring in buildings, yards, parking areas, and similar locations, and the kinds it does not cover, such as most utility-owned generation and distribution installations, ships, railway rolling stock, and mining equipment. It also covers installations where the Code applies only with special permission from the authority having jurisdiction. Smoke and carbon monoxide alarms in a house are handled by the building code, not by this article.
sections.on_the_job: The line that matters most in the field is the utility line: work on the customer side of the service point is generally Code work; the utility's own system generally is not. If a job sits in the not-covered or special-permission area, stop and get the AHJ's position before wiring it.

sections.title: How the chapters are arranged
sections.plain_explanation: Chapters 1 through 4 apply broadly to electrical installations. Chapters 5, 6 and 7 cover special places, special equipment and special conditions, and they add to or modify the general chapters. Chapter 8 covers communications systems and stands apart — the general chapters only apply to it where a Chapter 8 rule points back to them. Chapter 9 holds tables used by the rest of the book, and the annexes at the back are explanatory, not requirements.
sections.on_the_job: For a normal house or light-commercial job you live in Chapters 1 to 4. Open Chapter 5, 6 or 7 only when the occupancy or equipment is special, and when you do, read that rule together with the general rule it modifies.

sections.title: Enforcement and the AHJ
sections.plain_explanation:
The authority having jurisdiction — the AHJ — is the organization, office or individual responsible for enforcing the Code and approving equipment, materials and installations. On Florida work that is usually the local building department and its electrical inspectors.
• The AHJ interprets the rules and decides how they apply to a local situation.
• The AHJ approves equipment and installations, and enforces correction of work that does not comply.
• Where the Code allows an alternative, the AHJ can grant special permission — its written consent.
An inspector's reading on your job carries weight that a handbook, an app or a study guide does not.
sections.on_the_job: If a rule could be read two ways on a real job, ask the AHJ before rough-in, not at inspection. Write down who said what and when. The 210.8(F) protection question for outdoor HVAC outlets has been enforced differently by different Florida AHJs, so on a service change Sharma gets the local inspector's position first instead of arguing it at the final. This book is a reference aid; the AHJ and the printed NEC govern.
sections.florida_note: Local amendments and AHJ positions always win over a statewide summary, especially on items where enforcement has varied, such as GFCI protection for outdoor HVAC outlets under 210.8(F).

sections.title: Mandatory rules, permissive rules, and explanatory material
sections.plain_explanation:
The Code is written in three kinds of language, and 90.5 tells you how to read each one:
• Mandatory rules — 90.5(A): the words shall or shall not. These must be followed; there is no judgment call.
• Permissive rules — 90.5(B): the words shall be permitted or shall not be required. These allow an option; they never require it.
• Explanatory material — 90.5(C): Informational Notes and other material that explains a rule or points to other material. A note by itself does not create a requirement you can be failed for, and you cannot use a note to override a rule.
When a rule itself references another standard, that reference is part of the rule. The enforceable requirement always lives in the rule text, or in another standard the rule points to — never in the note.
sections.on_the_job: When someone cites a note as the reason for a red tag or a change, ask for the rule section behind it. Notes are where good explanations live, but the enforceable requirement is always in the rule text or in another standard the rule points to. On a Marion County service call, a homeowner insists a note under a receptacle rule means his garage conversion does not need GFCI protection. The note explains the rule; it does not repeal it — the shall in the rule text decides, and the receptacles get protected. The flip side on the same job: where the Code says a method shall be permitted, nobody can fail you for choosing it just because they prefer another method.

sections.why_it_exists: Reading a note as a rule, or a permission as a requirement, costs real money and can cost safety. Crews have torn out compliant work because someone treated an Informational Note like a shall, and jobs have stalled while a note was argued as if it could cancel a rule. Knowing which kind of language is speaking tells you what can be enforced, what is optional, and what is only there to help.
sections.exam_trap: The trap answer starts with “the Informational Note requires…” — a note never requires anything. The second trap reads “shall be permitted” as “shall”: a permissive rule allows the method, it does not force it onto every job.

sections.title: Formal interpretations
sections.plain_explanation:
Where there is a genuine dispute about what a Code rule means, there is a formal process for getting an official interpretation from NFPA. That process is slow and is meant for real disagreements about the text, not for settling a question on one job. One job's question goes to its AHJ.
• A formal interpretation is NFPA's official reading of the text itself, reached through its committee process. It speaks to the rule, for everyone.
• It does not decide your permit, your inspection or your job, and it does not arrive on a job's schedule.
• A magazine article, a handbook commentary or a forum post is not a formal interpretation, however confident it sounds.
For the job in front of you, the AHJ interprets how the rule applies (90.4), and that reading governs the job.
sections.on_the_job: You will almost never use this section in the field. Know that it exists so you do not treat a magazine article or a forum post as an official interpretation. If an inspector in Marion County reads a rule differently than you do, that is not a 90.6 fight: ask the AHJ, get the reading in writing when the job turns on it, and build to it.
sections.why_it_exists: One official channel keeps one meaning for the text. Without it, the same rule would read differently in every county, and a contractor could shop for the interpretation he likes. The formal process settles the words themselves, while the AHJ system keeps day-to-day calls fast and local — and it stops unofficial opinions from quietly becoming 'the Code' on a job.
sections.exam_trap: The trap answer sends a question about one job to NFPA for a formal interpretation. Wrong road: formal interpretations settle genuine disputes about the text itself, slowly, and for everyone. The question on the job in front of you goes to its AHJ, whose interpretation governs that job (90.4).

No AHJ interpretation on file for a disputed detail the whole job was built around.

sections.title: Examination of equipment for safety
sections.plain_explanation:
This section explains how equipment gets examined for safety, normally by being tested and listed or labeled by a qualified testing laboratory. It is the background for the approval, listing and labeling language used all through Article 110. Equipment the AHJ accepts has normally been through that kind of third-party check.
• Listed — the product appears in the testing organization's published list of items it has evaluated.
• Labeled — the organization has attached its label after checking samples of the product.
• Approved — acceptable to the AHJ (110.2). Listing and labeling are how approval is normally shown.
The point of the system: somebody qualified, who does not sell the product, has tested it against a safety standard before it reaches your job.
sections.on_the_job: Look for the listing mark and the label when gear arrives. If a piece of equipment has no mark and no paperwork, raise it before it is installed, not after it is wired. On a Sharma job, check the Siemens gear (S-02) at delivery: mark on the equipment, label readable, instructions in the box. A familiar brand is not the check — the specific piece of equipment still has to be listed and used within its listing.
sections.sharma_note: Sharma standard gear is Siemens (S-02). A listing problem is not solved by a familiar brand name — the specific equipment still has to be listed and used within its listing.
sections.figure_idea: Close-up style drawing of a panel label area with the listing mark, ratings and manufacturer instructions called out.
sections.why_it_exists: Untested gear can fail in ways nobody can see on a ladder: insulation that breaks down, parts that run hot, an enclosure that does not contain a fault. Third-party examination catches those defects before the equipment is hanging on a customer's wall, and it gives the AHJ something definite to approve instead of an opinion about a brand.
sections.exam_trap: The trap is treating a famous brand name, or a seller's assurance, as proof of safety. The 90.7 system runs on examination by a qualified testing laboratory: listed, labeled, and approved by the AHJ. No mark and no paperwork means the question goes up before the gear goes in — not after the inspection fails.

sections.title: Planning for future expansion
sections.plain_explanation:
Section 90.8 has two halves that work very differently:
• 90.8(A) — planning for expansion. Plan an installation so later growth in load does not require tearing the system apart. Allowing room for future circuits and capacity is presented as good practice, for convenience and for the life of the installation — encouragement, not a hard sizing rule. No percentage of spare capacity is mandated here.
• 90.8(B) — the number of circuits in enclosures. This half is a hard rule: an enclosure may not be filled beyond the number of circuits it was designed and listed to hold. The panel's listing, not the number of breakers that can physically be forced in, sets the limit.
Read together: leave room because it is smart, and never overfill because it is prohibited.
sections.on_the_job: Spare panel spaces, an accessible junction point, and a raceway path that can be reused are cheap on rough-in day and expensive later. On a Marion Oaks new build we set a 200 A Siemens panel with 40 spaces, landed 29 circuits, and left 11 spaces open, with a spare conduit stubbed from the panel into the attic for the pool equipment the owner plans next year. When that job comes, the next electrician — often us — has a workable path instead of a change-out quote. Where the plan allows, leave that path.
sections.why_it_exists: Loads only grow — the EV charger, the pool, the addition, the workshop. A panel stuffed full on day one turns every later job into a change-out, and an enclosure filled past its listed circuit count is a listing violation waiting for an inspector or a failure. Planning room at rough-in costs almost nothing; creating it later costs a service call, a permit, and a day.
sections.exam_trap: The trap answer turns 90.8(A) into a mandate: "The Code requires 25 percent spare panel capacity." It does not. Section 90.8(A) encourages planning for expansion; it sets no percentage and sizes nothing. The enforceable half of the section is (B): fill an enclosure beyond the number of circuits it was designed and listed to hold, and you have a violation — however neat the tandem breakers look.

sections.title: Units of measurement
sections.plain_explanation:
Every measurement in the Code is printed twice: a metric (SI) value and an inch-pound value. The pair is joined by soft conversion — each side is rounded to a clean number in its own system — so the two do not convert exactly:
• The 3 ft working-space depth is printed as 900 mm. Converted exactly, 3 ft is 914 mm.
• The 3 ft 6 in depth is printed as 1.0 m; the exact conversion is 1.07 m.
• The 4 ft depth is printed as 1.2 m; the exact conversion is 1.22 m.
• The 6½ ft headroom is printed as 2.0 m; the exact conversion is 1.98 m.
Neither printed value is a misprint, and one inch is exactly 25.4 mm — the rounding is deliberate. Build to the value printed in the rule you are using, in the system your tape reads. In United States field work, that is the inch-pound value.
sections.on_the_job: Measure in inches and feet as printed in the rule you are using. On a small commercial job, a metric set of plans shows the panel working space at 900 mm; the crew tapes 3 ft, and it is the same box the inspector measures, because the Code prints the pair together. The miss to avoid is converting 900 mm back to 35.4 in and taping the shallower number. Do not convert a Code dimension yourself and then argue from your conversion at inspection.

Let each installer convert for himself and the roundings stack in both directions — one man's 900 mm becomes another man's 35 in — and the argument lands at inspection, where the printed rule was going to win anyway.

The printed value, in the system you are measuring in, is the requirement — your calculator does not outrank the book.

sections.title: Article 100 — Definitions: the words the Code uses
sections.plain_explanation:
Article 100 defines the terms that carry a special meaning inside the Code. When a defined word appears in a rule, it means what Article 100 says it means, even if the everyday meaning is broader or narrower. In the 2020 edition the definitions sit in three parts — general definitions, definitions for installations over 1000 volts, and definitions for hazardous (classified) locations — arranged alphabetically inside each part rather than as numbered sections. This chapter covers the job-critical general terms a Sharma helper meets first; it does not attempt every definition in the article.

sections.title: Accessible and readily accessible
sections.plain_explanation:
Article 100 uses the word two ways, and then adds a stricter version:
• Accessible (equipment): a person can get close to it to operate, inspect or maintain it, without being blocked by the building's permanent structure.
• Accessible (wiring method): it can be removed or reached without tearing out finished construction — nothing buried behind the finish.
• Readily accessible: stricter. A person can get to it quickly, without tools other than a key, without climbing over obstacles, and without a portable ladder.
The everyday test: if reaching it means demolition, it is not accessible. If reaching it means fetching a ladder and moving storage, it is not readily accessible.
sections.on_the_job: A breaker behind a locked door the occupant can open is different from a junction box buried behind drywall. Buried boxes are the classic failure: a wiring method that cannot be reached without demolition is not accessible, and splices belong in accessible boxes. On a remodel in The Villages, the previous electrician buried a junction box behind new drywall, found only because a circuit died. The box gets cut open and relocated into an accessible box with a blank cover — the splice was fine, the burial was not. The garage subpanel on the same job, behind a door the homeowner opens with a key and with clear floor in front, passes both tests.
sections.figure_idea: Two panels: one reached by a clear path marked readily accessible, one behind stored shelving and a ladder marked not readily accessible.
sections.why_it_exists: Equipment that cannot be reached cannot be maintained, inspected, or shut off in a hurry. A splice buried behind drywall fails silently for years — heat and arcing with no way to find it short of opening the wall. The readily accessible line is about routine work as much as emergencies: the person who needs that breaker or disconnect should not need a ladder, a toolbox and a scavenger hunt to get there.
sections.exam_trap: The trap is treating accessible and readily accessible as the same word. Accessible is the low bar — you can get there without demolition. Readily accessible adds speed: no tools other than a key, no climbing over or under obstacles, no portable ladder. A disconnect you can only reach by ladder may be accessible, but where the Code says readily accessible, it fails.

sections.title: Ampacity
sections.plain_explanation:
Ampacity is the most current, in amperes, a conductor can carry continuously in its actual conditions of use without getting hotter than its temperature rating allows. It is not a single number printed on the wire; it depends on the conductor material, insulation rating, ambient temperature, and how many current-carrying conductors share a raceway or cable.
• Start in Table 310.16, in the column the insulation type and the terminations allow.
• Then correct for ambient heat (310.15(B)) and adjust for bundled current-carrying conductors (310.15(C)(1)).
• Worked example: 12 AWG THHN copper starts at 30 A in the 90 °C column. In a 104 °F space (×0.91) with four current-carrying conductors (×0.80) it adjusts to 21.8 A — and 240.4(D) still caps the breaker at 20 A.
sections.on_the_job: Start from Table 310.16, then adjust for the job's real conditions. A conductor that is fine alone in a cool space can be over its limit bundled in a hot Florida attic. One Sharma home run: two 20 A circuits of 12 AWG THHN copper in one EMT through a 104 °F mechanical space — four current-carrying conductors. The math runs 30 A × 0.91 × 0.80 = 21.8 A, which stays above the 20 A breaker, so the circuit stands. Add a third circuit to that pipe, or route it through a hotter attic, and the same wire no longer works.
sections.sharma_note: S-10: CCA is rated from the aluminum column of Table 310.16, which is why Sharma goes one AWG size larger when CCA is used.
sections.figure_idea: Cross-section of a conductor with heat arrows leaving it: ampacity is set by the heat the insulation can take, not by the copper alone.
sections.florida_note: Florida attic temperatures make ambient correction a real design step, not a paperwork exercise.

sections.why_it_exists: Current makes heat, and heat is what kills insulation — slowly, inside walls, years after the inspection sign-off. Ampacity is the line between a conductor that runs warm for decades and one whose insulation cracks, faults, and starts a fire in a stud bay. Florida attics run far past the 30 °C the table assumes, so the correction step is where Florida jobs are won or lost.
inspection_fails: Conductors sized straight from the 90 °C column with no ambient correction in a hot attic (310.15(B)).
More than three current-carrying conductors in a raceway with no adjustment applied (310.15(C)(1)).
12 AWG copper on a 25 A or 30 A breaker because 'THHN is good for 30 A' (240.4(D)).
NM cable ampacity taken from the 90 °C column — 334.80 holds it to the 60 °C result.
sections.exam_trap: The trap is quoting the 90 °C column as the final answer: '12 AWG THHN is a 30 A wire.' The 90 °C value is only the starting point for correction and adjustment. The terminations pull the usable value into their own column, and 240.4(D) caps the breaker at 20 A no matter what the arithmetic produces.

sections.title: Conductors — bare, covered, insulated, and the neutral
sections.plain_explanation: Article 100 sorts conductors by what is on the metal. A bare conductor has no covering or insulation at all. A covered conductor has a covering that is not recognized insulation — it may protect against weather or abrasion, but it earns the wire no insulation rating. An insulated conductor has insulation that is recognized for the use, which is the normal building wire a crew handles. The neutral conductor is the conductor connected to the system's neutral point that is intended to carry current under normal conditions; the neutral point is the common point of a wye connection, or the midpoint of a single-phase or DC system, from which the circuit conductors are referenced.
sections.on_the_job: Do not treat a covered conductor as insulated when a rule calls for insulation — service-drop covering is the classic example. And the neutral is a current-carrying working conductor, not a spare ground: it lands on the neutral bar and is only bonded to ground where the Code allows the bond.
sections.figure_idea: Three wire cross-sections side by side: bare metal, a weather covering, and full insulation, with the neutral point of a wye drawn beside them.

sections.title: Voltage — nominal voltage, voltage to ground, and circuit voltage
sections.plain_explanation: Three voltage terms run through the whole Code. Voltage of a circuit is the greatest difference of potential between any two conductors of that circuit. Nominal voltage is the value the system is named by — 120, 240, 480 — used to classify circuits and equipment even though the actual voltage wanders a little above and below it. Voltage to ground is the voltage between a conductor and the earth or the grounded point of the system: on a 120/240V house service it is 120V, and on a 208Y/120V system it is 120V, which is why so many clearance and working-space rules key on it instead of the phase-to-phase number.
sections.on_the_job: When a table asks for voltage to ground, answer with the leg-to-ground number, not the nameplate of the service. A 120/240V panel sits in the 0–150V-to-ground row even though 240V appears across its bus.

sections.title: Appliance
sections.plain_explanation:
An appliance is utilization equipment, usually built as a unit, that does a household or similar job — cooking, washing, drying, comfort heating or cooling, and the like — other than a basic luminaire or motor by itself. The word matters because several branch-circuit and disconnect rules turn on whether the load is an appliance.
• Appliances: dishwashers, disposals, ranges, cooktops, dryers, built-in microwaves, storage water heaters.
• Not appliances standing alone: a luminaire, a motor by itself, or a receptacle outlet. Each of those has its own article.
• When the load is an appliance, Article 422 switches on: sizing from the marked rating, an individual branch circuit as the default for the big fixed appliances (422.10), the marked maximum overcurrent device (422.11), and GFCI protection that travels with the appliance for the 422.5(A) list.
sections.on_the_job: Marion Oaks kitchen, rough-in day: the dishwasher and the disposal are both appliances, so they are planned as appliance loads, not as spare receptacle outlets. The built-in microwave gets its own 20 A circuit (Sharma S-06), and the dishwasher gets GFCI protection under 422.5 — that duty travels with the appliance and sits on top of the kitchen receptacle rules in 210.8. Before trim, walk the kitchen and name every appliance out loud. The ones nobody names are the ones that get wired like outlets.
sections.sharma_note: S-06 is PENDING. The microwave gets its own 20A circuit. The wire is not settled — 12 AWG copper versus 10 AWG CCA — until Mike Holt rules. If the plan or the nameplate states a size, that statement governs.

Treat a dishwasher like an ordinary receptacle load and you can miss the GFCI protection 422.5 requires wherever that appliance is installed. Treat a plain luminaire like an appliance and you apply rules that were never written for it. The name of the load decides which rulebook opens, so the name has to be right first.

Wrong — it is an appliance, Article 422 applies, and 422.5 puts GFCI protection on it wherever it is installed. The mirror-image trap calls a bare motor or a luminaire an appliance. sections.title: Approved, identified, labeled, and listed
sections.plain_explanation:
These four words form one family, and they are not interchangeable:
• Approved means acceptable to the authority having jurisdiction. The AHJ has the final say on the installation.
• Identified means recognizable as suitable for the specific purpose, function, use, environment, or application in question — fit for this use, not just some use.
• Labeled means a testing organization has attached its label or other identifying mark to the product, after checking samples of it.
• Listed means the product appears in that organization's published list of items it has evaluated.
A product can be well made and still not be listed, and an unlisted product used where listing is required is a Code problem. The chain also runs one way: the lab lists and labels, but only the AHJ approves.
sections.on_the_job: Read the box and the device. On a panel change in Ocala, the supply house substituted a breaker of another brand that physically snapped into the new Siemens panel. It fit — and it was not identified for that panel, so it came back out. Breakers must be listed and identified for the panel they go in; a breaker that physically fits a foreign panel is not thereby identified for it. That is exactly what S-02 and S-03 are for: Siemens in Siemens, Square D in Square D.
sections.sharma_note: S-02: all new gear is Siemens. S-03: in an existing Square D panel, use Square D breakers listed for that panel — never mix brands to fill a space.
sections.figure_idea: Four stacked badges showing the chain: tested by a lab, listed in its directory, labeled on the product, approved by the AHJ for the job.
sections.why_it_exists: These words are how the Code trusts equipment it has never seen. Listing and labeling mean an independent lab actually evaluated the product; identified ties it to the exact job in front of you; approval puts the local AHJ's judgment on top. Skip a link — an unlisted import, a breaker from the wrong panel family — and nobody has verified the gear will fail safely instead of burning.
sections.exam_trap: The trap swaps the family members. "Approved" does not mean the lab tested it — it means acceptable to the AHJ. "Listed" is not the sticker on the product — the sticker is the label; listed means the product stands in the lab's published list. And "it fits and it works" never makes a device identified for a use it was not evaluated for.

sections.title: Equipment, utilization equipment, enclosures, and fittings
sections.plain_explanation: Equipment is the Code's umbrella word for the apparatus of an installation — fittings, devices, appliances, luminaires, machines and the like, whether they carry current or just support the parts that do. Utilization equipment is the narrower slice that actually uses electric energy to do work: heating, lighting, cooling, data processing and similar jobs. An enclosure is the case or housing around apparatus that keeps people away from live parts and protects the contents; enclosed describes apparatus that has such a case. A fitting is an accessory — a locknut, bushing or similar part — that does a mechanical job rather than an electrical one. A handhole enclosure is a small below-grade access enclosure, set flush or buried, whose cover a worker removes by hand to reach the conductors inside.
sections.on_the_job: Calling something 'equipment' is what brings the Article 110 rules with it — approval, working space, guarding. Handholes are the buried splice points on site work: they are enclosures, so the splices inside still have to be made with listed methods and the cover kept accessible, not paved over.

sections.title: Bonding — bonded, bonding conductor, bonding jumper
sections.plain_explanation:
Bonded means connected to establish electrical continuity and conductivity. Bonding is the act of joining metal parts together so they hold the same electrical potential and share a reliable, low-impedance path that can carry fault current back to the source.
• Bonding jumper: the conductor or fitting that makes a bonding connection
• Main bonding jumper: the connection at the service between the grounded conductor (the neutral) and the equipment grounding side
• Equipment bonding jumper: the jumper that ties equipment enclosures and raceways into that path
Bonding is not grounding. The grounding electrode — the rod, the Ufer, the water pipe — connects the system to the earth, and earth is a poor conductor that will not clear a fault. Bonding's job is metal-to-metal: give fault current a hard, fast path home so the breaker trips.
sections.on_the_job: Metal boxes, raceways, enclosures and equipment frames that can become energized need a bonding path back to the source. A loose locknut or paint under a fitting can quietly break that path. Picture a 20 A kitchen circuit: the hot conductor chafes through on the edge of a metal box. With the box bonded, the fault current rushes back to the panel and the breaker opens. With paint under the locknut and the locknut finger-tight, the same box sits live at 120 V — and the first person to learn about it is the one who touches it and a grounded sink at the same time.
sections.figure_idea: A metal box and raceway with the fault-current path highlighted returning to the panel, separate from the ground rod path to earth.
sections.why_it_exists: Without a bonding path, a hot wire faulted to a metal box leaves that box sitting at line voltage, silent, waiting for a hand. The breaker never trips because the fault current has nowhere strong to flow. Bonding turns that silent, energized box into a heavy fault the breaker clears at once.
inspection_fails: Bonding fitting landed over paint or drywall compound — nonconductive coatings left in place where they break the fault path.
Locknuts finger-tight on a service raceway — the bonding path depends on a wrench-tight, listed connection.
Metal raceway run interrupted by a plastic box or fitting with no bonding jumper around it.
No bonding jumper across a water meter or a dielectric union — the piping path is broken at the joint.
sections.exam_trap: The trap answer bonds equipment by driving a ground rod next to it. A rod connects to the earth; it does not give fault current the low-impedance metal path back to the source that trips the breaker. Bonding and grounding are two different jobs that happen to meet at the service.

sections.title: Grounding conductors and electrodes — EGC, GEC, and bonding jumpers
sections.plain_explanation: The grounding family splits by job. The equipment grounding conductor (EGC) connects the metal frames of equipment back to the source so a ground fault becomes a big fault current that trips the breaker — it is usually the green or bare wire, but 250.118 also lets certain raceways and cable armor serve as the EGC.. The grounding electrode conductor (GEC) connects the system to the grounding electrode — the rod, plate, concrete-encased electrode or other recognized earth connection itself. The main bonding jumper is the connection at the service between the grounded conductor and the EGC side; a system bonding jumper does the same job at a separately derived system. The existing Bonding and Grounded/Grounding pages cover the base words; this page is the conductor-by-conductor map.
sections.on_the_job: Mixing up the EGC and the GEC is the classic exam and inspection trap: the EGC protects people from energized metal, the GEC connects the system to earth, and they are sized from different tables (250.122 for the EGC, 250.66 for the GEC). In a normal house the only neutral-to-ground bond is the main bonding jumper at the service; a separately derived system (for example a transformer or a generator switched as an SDS) gets its own system bonding jumper, and downstream panels keep neutral and ground separate. — downstream panels keep them separate.

sections.title: Grounded and grounding — telling the conductors apart
sections.plain_explanation:
Two words that sound almost the same do two completely different jobs, and Article 100 defines them separately on purpose:
• Grounded: connected to the earth, or to a conductive body that extends the earth connection.
• Grounded conductor: a system or circuit conductor that is intentionally grounded. In a house that is the neutral — white or gray — and it carries normal load current every day.
• Grounding conductor: a conductor used to connect equipment or the grounded circuit conductor to a grounding electrode or to a point on the grounding electrode system.
• Equipment grounding conductor (EGC): the conductive path that ties equipment enclosures, raceways and other non-current-carrying metal parts to the system grounded conductor and the electrode, so fault current can get back to the source and trip the breaker.
• Grounding electrode conductor (GEC): the conductor that connects the system grounded conductor, or the equipment, to the grounding electrode.
The one-sentence test: the grounded conductor works every day carrying load current; the grounding conductors sit idle until something goes wrong.
sections.on_the_job: On a 200 A house service in Marion Oaks, the white grounded conductor lands on the neutral bar, and the bare GEC runs from that same bar out to the ground rods — the service is the one place the two systems are bonded together, through the main bonding jumper. Every subpanel Sharma sets downstream keeps them apart: neutrals on an insulated bar, green and bare equipment grounding conductors on the ground bar, no bonding screw. On the branch circuits the white wire carries the load current home; the green or bare wire carries nothing until a fault, then it carries the fault back so the breaker opens.
sections.figure_idea: Panel detail with the neutral bar and ground bar labelled grounded vs grounding, and the single bonding point at the service marked.
sections.why_it_exists: Mix the two up and people get hurt. A neutral landed on the ground bar downstream of the service puts load current on metal enclosures and raceways, so pipes and panel covers sit energized all day. A missing grounding path does the opposite harm: a fault has no low-impedance road back to the source, the breaker never trips, and the enclosure stays live, waiting for a hand.
sections.exam_trap: The exam loves the near-identical names. The trap answer treats “grounded conductor” and “grounding conductor” as interchangeable, or calls the white wire the grounding conductor. Remember it by the job, not the sound: grounded = the neutral that works daily; grounding = the safety path that works only on a fault.

sections.title: Ground fault, GFCI, and ground-fault protection of equipment
sections.plain_explanation: A ground fault is an unintended connection between an ungrounded conductor and normally non-current-carrying metal or the earth — the fault the EGC exists to turn into a breaker trip. Two protective terms build on it and are not interchangeable. A ground-fault circuit interrupter (GFCI) protects people: it watches for current leaking outside the intended path and opens the circuit at a few milliamperes, the personnel-protection level (a Class A GFCI must trip when ground-fault current reaches 6 mA and must not trip below 4 mA — Art. 100 GFCI Informational Note, from UL 943).. Ground-fault protection of equipment (GFPE) protects equipment and conductors from damaging fault currents at much higher levels — hundreds of amperes on large services — and is not intended to protect a person from shock.
sections.on_the_job: A GFPE breaker on a big service will not save a helper who contacts a live part, and a receptacle GFCI is not equipment protection for a service. When a spec or an inspector says 'ground-fault protection,' ask which of the two is meant before ordering gear.

sections.title: Branch circuit
sections.plain_explanation:
A branch circuit is the part of the wiring system between the final overcurrent device protecting it — the breaker in the panel — and the outlets it feeds. Everything upstream of that breaker is a feeder or service conductor; everything downstream to the receptacles, lights and equipment is the branch circuit. Article 210 builds its rules on this definition.
• It starts at that circuit's final overcurrent device — not at the meter, and not at the panel as a whole.
• It ends at the outlets: receptacle outlets, lighting outlets, and hard-wired equipment.
• Feeders feed panels; branch circuits feed loads. The same wire can be either one, depending on where the final breaker sits.
sections.on_the_job: When you size, protect or troubleshoot a circuit, find its breaker first. The conductor size, the breaker rating and the outlets all have to agree as one branch circuit. On a Sharma commercial job that agreement has a floor: every branch circuit is 20 A minimum on 12 AWG copper minimum (S-01), even where the Code would allow a 15 A circuit. On a house call, a dead bedroom receptacle is a branch-circuit problem — start at its breaker in the panel, not at the service.
sections.sharma_note: S-01: on commercial work every branch circuit is 20A minimum on 12 AWG copper minimum — no 15A branch circuits on commercial jobs. That is Sharma practice, stricter than the Code floor.
sections.figure_idea: One-line diagram: a breaker in the panel and the run out to the outlets it feeds, shaded as the branch circuit.

sections.why_it_exists: The boundary decides which rules size the wire and which device protects the load. Feeder rules and branch-circuit rules are different articles with different math. Call a run by the wrong name and you can protect a load with a device that was only ever meant to feed a panel — or hunt a dead receptacle at the meter when the whole problem is one tripped breaker.

Multiwire branch circuit with no means to disconnect all ungrounded conductors at once (210.4(B)).
sections.exam_trap: The trap answer starts the branch circuit at the service disconnect, or at the panel itself. It starts at the final overcurrent device for that circuit. A breaker in the main panel that feeds a garage subpanel is a feeder breaker, not the final device — the garage branch circuits begin at the breakers in the subpanel.

sections.title: Branch-circuit types — appliance, general purpose, individual, multiwire
sections.plain_explanation: Article 100 names four branch-circuit types. An appliance branch circuit feeds energy-utilizing equipment other than luminaires. A general purpose branch circuit feeds two or more receptacles or outlets for lighting and appliances. An individual branch circuit feeds only one piece of utilization equipment. A multiwire branch circuit uses two or more ungrounded conductors that have a voltage between them, sharing one grounded (neutral) conductor that carries only the unbalanced difference between them — the shared-neutral circuit a crew meets on kitchen and homerun work. The base Branch circuit page covers where a branch circuit starts and ends; this page is the family tree.
sections.on_the_job: The shared neutral is what makes a multiwire circuit efficient and dangerous at the same time: open that neutral under load and the two legs go in series across 240V, over-volting one side. Both legs must disconnect together, and the conductors must land on opposite legs — same-leg 'sharing' overloads the neutral instead of cancelling.
sections.figure_idea: Four simple one-line diagrams, one per type, with the multiwire circuit showing two hots sharing one neutral.

sections.title: Circuit breaker, panelboard, cabinet, and the fault ratings
sections.plain_explanation: A circuit breaker is a device that opens and closes a circuit by nonautomatic means and opens it automatically at a preset overcurrent — an adjustable-trip breaker lets that trip setting be changed without swapping internal parts. A panelboard is a single panel, or group of panel units, of switches or breakers in a cabinet, designed to mount in or against a wall; the enclosure is a cabinet or a cutout box — two separately defined terms (a cabinet has a frame/trim for a swinging door; a cutout box has a door or cover hinged directly to the box walls)., surface or flush, with doors or trim as designed. Two fault ratings live here and are constantly confused: interrupting rating is the highest fault current a device itself can safely open at its rated voltage; short-circuit current rating (SCCR) is the fault current a piece of equipment as a whole can withstand or be protected at. The 110.9 and 110.10 pages carry the rules behind both ratings.
sections.on_the_job: A breaker that fits is not a breaker that belongs: its interrupting rating must meet or beat the available fault current at its terminals, and the panel's SCCR must cover the installation — check the labels before the gear is set, not at inspection.
sections.figure_idea: A panelboard cutaway: breakers inside, cabinet around them, with callouts for the interrupting rating on a breaker label and the SCCR on the panel label.

sections.title: Feeder
sections.plain_explanation: A feeder is the set of circuit conductors between the service equipment, or another power supply source such as a separately derived system, and the final branch-circuit overcurrent devices. It is the middle layer of the system: service conductors feed the service equipment, feeders carry power onward to panels, and branch circuits run from those panels' breakers to the outlets. Rules for sizing, protection and grounding change depending on which layer a conductor belongs to.
sections.on_the_job: The house-to-detached-garage panel run is the everyday feeder: it starts at an overcurrent device in the house panel and ends at the breakers in the garage panel. Call a run by its right layer before applying any sizing or grounding rule to it.
sections.figure_idea: One-line diagram: service equipment feeding a subpanel, the run between them shaded as the feeder and the branch circuits beyond left unshaded.

sections.title: Continuous load
sections.plain_explanation:
A continuous load is a load where the maximum current is expected to keep flowing for 3 hours or more at a stretch. The three-hour line is the whole definition.
• Expected to continue — the test is the load's normal pattern, not one unusual long day.
• At maximum current — a load that cycles is judged by what it actually holds; cycling equipment may not be continuous at all.
• The definition sets no size by itself. The sizing rules that use the term do: a continuous load is counted at 125 percent for conductor and overcurrent sizing (210.19(A)(1), 210.20(A)), unless the assembly is listed for operation at 100 percent of its rating.
So a 40 A load that runs 3 hours or more is counted as 40 × 1.25 = 50 A before the wire or the breaker is picked.
sections.on_the_job: Lighting in a store that stays on all day, an EV charger, and long-running HVAC loads are the usual suspects. Ask how long the load actually runs before deciding whether the continuous-load treatment applies. Worked case: a home EV charger pulling 40 A through the night is continuous — 40 × 1.25 = 50 A, so it is built as a 50 A circuit, not a 40 A one. A storage water heater gets the same treatment from its own article, at 125 percent of nameplate (422.13).
sections.figure_idea: A timeline graphic: a load running 2 hours marked noncontinuous, the same load running 3 hours and beyond marked continuous.
sections.why_it_exists: Heat is the reason. A conductor and a breaker carrying full current for hours reach their full working temperature and stay there — there is no cool-down between cycles. Counting the load at 125 percent buys the thermal margin that keeps terminations and insulation at the temperature they were rated for, all day, every day.
sections.exam_trap: The trap misses the line in both directions. Maximum current for 2 hours is not continuous — the line is 3 hours. And a load that runs all day at half its maximum is not 'continuous at maximum' either: the definition needs maximum current, expected, for 3 hours or more. Get the definition right first; the 125 percent sizing follows from it.
inspection_fails: EV charger on a circuit sized at nameplate amps only — no 125 percent for the continuous load.
Store lighting circuit loaded to the breaker's full rating; the breaker runs hot and nuisance-trips by mid-afternoon.
Water heater circuit figured at nameplate with no 125 percent (422.13).
Conductor sized to the load while the breaker was sized at 125 percent — the two halves of the calc disagree.

figures.alt: Timeline diagram comparing two loads: one running at maximum current for 2 hours stays under the gold 3-hour line and is not continuous, while the same load running 3 hours or more crosses the line, is a continuous load, and is sized at 125 percent.
figures.caption: The 3-hour line is the whole definition.

sections.title: Demand factor, nonlinear load, and overcurrent
sections.plain_explanation: Demand factor is the ratio of the maximum demand of a system (or part of one) to the total connected load — it is always 1.0 or less, and it is what lets a feeder be smaller than the sum of everything plugged into it, because not everything runs at once. A nonlinear load is a load whose current waveform does not follow the voltage waveform — LED drivers, electronic ballasts, variable-speed drives and most plug-in electronics — which pushes harmonic current onto the system, especially the shared neutral. Overcurrent is any current above a conductor's or equipment's rating, from either of two causes crews must tell apart: an overload is too much legitimate load in an otherwise sound circuit, while a short circuit or ground fault is a failure — the protection and the troubleshooting are different for each.
sections.on_the_job: Demand factor is why the service math in Chapter 2 never just adds every breaker. Nonlinear loads are why a shared neutral on a multiwire circuit feeding LED lighting may need to be treated as current-carrying and sometimes upsized — the harmonics add on the neutral instead of cancelling.
sections.figure_idea: A bar chart: connected load tall, maximum demand shorter, the ratio labelled demand factor; beside it a distorted current waveform labelled nonlinear.

sections.title: Dwelling unit
sections.plain_explanation:
A dwelling unit is one unit that gives one or more people complete, independent living facilities. The definition has four functions, and all four must be there, with permanent provisions:
• Living — a real living space
• Sleeping — permanent sleeping quarters
• Cooking — permanent cooking provisions, not a plug-in hot plate
• Sanitation — a bathroom
Miss one and the space is not a dwelling unit. The label matters because a long list of house rules in the Code switches on or off with it: receptacle spacing (210.52), GFCI protection (210.8(A)), the required branch circuits (210.11(C)), AFCI protection (210.12) and the dwelling load calculation in Article 220 all key off this one definition.
sections.on_the_job: A one-family house in Marion Oaks is a dwelling unit, and so is every apartment in a multifamily building. So is a Kissimmee house rented out nightly as a vacation rental — rented or owned, it still provides complete living facilities, so the dwelling rules apply in full, including the 210.52 wall-space rule (no point along the floor line more than 6 ft from a receptacle). A pool house with day beds and a wet bar is not a dwelling unit: no permanent cooking and no bathroom. Add a real kitchenette and a full bath to that pool house and it becomes one — and the GFCI, AFCI and spacing rules switch on with it.
sections.figure_idea: Cutaway of one home: living, sleeping, cooking and sanitation together in a single unit behind one front door.
sections.why_it_exists: Dwelling rules are written for the hardest case: people asleep, children, and hours of unattended use around electricity. The definition draws the line between that kind of space and a room people only pass through, so the extra protection lands where people actually live.
inspection_fails: AFCI protection skipped in a short-term rental house because 'nobody lives there' — rented nightly, it is still a dwelling unit (210.12).
Dwelling living room roughed in to commercial spacing — no point along the floor line may sit more than 6 ft from a receptacle (210.52(A)).
Pool house finished with a permanent kitchenette and full bath — now a dwelling unit — with no GFCI or AFCI protection.
Dwelling rules applied to a hotel guest room with no permanent cooking, while the actual dwelling units on the same job were missed.
sections.exam_trap: The trap answer treats any room where somebody sleeps as a dwelling unit — a hotel room, a hospital room, a pool house with a fold-out bed. Sleeping alone is not enough. All four functions must be present with permanent provisions, and cooking is the one most often missing.

sections.title: Bathroom and clothes closet
sections.plain_explanation: A bathroom, in Article 100, is an area that includes a basin plus one or more of a toilet, a urinal, a tub, a shower, a bidet, or a similar plumbing fixture. — a room with only a toilet and no basin is not a bathroom under the Code, and a basin with nothing else is not either. The definition matters because whole rule sets switch on it: the 20A bathroom receptacle circuit, GFCI protection for bathroom receptacles, and the ban on receptacles inside tub and shower spaces. A clothes closet is the nonhabitable room or space meant for storing clothes — the definition behind the luminaire rules that keep hot, exposed lamps away from stored clothing and shelving.
sections.on_the_job: On plans, check the fixture list before applying bathroom rules: a powder room with a basin and toilet is a bathroom; a water closet alone is not. In closets, the clothes-closet definition is what triggers the luminaire type and clearance rules in 410.16 — treat any closet with a rod and shelf as one unless the plans say otherwise.

sections.title: Exposed — live parts and wiring methods
sections.plain_explanation:
Exposed has two uses.
• Exposed (as applied to live parts): a part can be accidentally touched or approached nearer than a safe distance — it is not properly guarded, isolated or insulated.
• Exposed (as applied to wiring methods): the wiring is on or against a surface, or behind panels meant to allow access, rather than permanently hidden inside the building structure.
The word matters because other rules key off it. Exposed live parts trigger the guarding rules; exposed wiring has to be protected where its own article requires it.
sections.on_the_job: Same garage, two different problems. The cable run on the surface of the garage wall is exposed wiring and needs the protection its article requires where it can be damaged. A live bus that a finger can reach is exposed live parts and is a guarding problem under Article 110 until the cover is back on or the parts are guarded. Both are correctly called 'exposed' — the fix is different for each, and naming which one you have is the first step of the repair.

Call a live part 'exposed' and the guarding rules of Article 110 wake up; call a wiring run 'exposed' and its article's protection rules apply. Read the word wrong and both hazards slip past: live parts a finger can reach, and surface cable left where it can be damaged.

sections.title: Concealed
sections.plain_explanation: Concealed describes wiring or equipment that is made inaccessible by the structure or finish of the building — behind drywall, above a finished ceiling, inside a slab. It is the mirror of the Exposed page: concealed does not mean hidden from the Code. Concealed work still has to be installed by the rules for the method, because once the finish goes on, nobody can inspect or reach it without demolition — which is exactly why rough-in inspection happens before cover.
sections.on_the_job: Anything concealed still has to be accessible where the Code demands access — junction boxes and splices may not be buried behind finish, the trap the Accessible page warns about. If a box will end up concealed and unreachable, move it or add an access panel before the drywall goes up.

sections.title: Locations — dry, damp, and wet
sections.plain_explanation: A dry location is one not normally damp or wet, though it can be temporarily damp during construction. A damp location is partly protected from weather or subject to moderate moisture — under a canopy, in some basements and barns, and similar places. A wet location is where water or other liquid can contact the equipment directly, or the installation is underground or in concrete or masonry in contact with the earth. The location decides what equipment and wiring methods are suitable.
sections.on_the_job: In Florida, treat exterior work as wet unless it is genuinely sheltered, and slabs and below-grade runs as wet by definition. Use equipment identified for the location you actually have, not the one you wish you had.
sections.figure_idea: Three house vignettes: an interior bedroom marked dry, a covered porch marked damp, an open exterior wall and a slab run marked wet.
sections.florida_note: Florida humidity and wind-driven rain push many borderline porch and carport locations toward damp or wet in the AHJ's judgment. Confirm borderline locations with the inspector rather than assuming dry.

sections.title: Weatherproof, watertight, and dusttight
sections.plain_explanation: Three enclosure-exposure terms, in rising order of sealing. Weatherproof means constructed or protected so that exposure to the weather does not interfere with successful operation — rain may reach it, but the equipment still works; it does not promise that water stays out. Watertight means constructed so moisture does not enter the enclosure under specified test conditions — the seal itself is the point. Dusttight means constructed so dust does not enter under specified test conditions. These sit alongside the Locations page: the location says how wet the place is, these terms say what the enclosure does about its environment.
sections.on_the_job: Weatherproof is the word that fools people — a weatherproof bell box sheds weather well enough to work, but it is not watertight, and neither word substitutes for the wet-location listing and in-use cover rules where those apply. Read the enclosure's actual rating for the job at hand.

sections.title: Outlet and receptacle
sections.plain_explanation: An outlet is any point on the wiring system where current is taken to feed utilization equipment — a receptacle point, a lighting point, a smoke-alarm point and a hardwired equipment connection are all outlets. A receptacle is the contact device installed at an outlet for plugging in a cord-connected load, and a receptacle outlet is an outlet where one or more receptacles are installed. Every receptacle is at an outlet, but not every outlet is a receptacle.
sections.on_the_job: Spacing and circuit rules that say outlet usually count lighting and hardwired points too, while rules that say receptacle outlet count only plug points. Mixing the two up is a common cause of a missed required receptacle or a wrong box-fill count.
sections.sharma_note: S-04: receptacle boxes sit 18 in to the bottom of the box when the plan is silent; when the plan states a height, the plan governs.
sections.figure_idea: A wall elevation with four outlets circled — receptacle, ceiling light, smoke alarm, hardwired dishwasher — and only the first labelled receptacle outlet.

sections.title: Luminaire and lighting outlet
sections.plain_explanation: A luminaire is the complete lighting unit — lamp or LED source, the parts that distribute the light, position and protect the source, and connect it to the supply. It is the Code's word for what crews call a fixture, and the Code uses luminaire everywhere a rule means the whole unit, not just the bulb. A lighting outlet is an outlet intended to connect directly to a luminaire or lampholder — one of the outlet types on the Outlet and receptacle page, and the point where the branch circuit's responsibility for that light ends.
sections.on_the_job: Fixture counts on a takeoff are luminaire counts. When a rule or a plan says 'lighting outlet,' it means the box and circuit point, whether or not the luminaire itself has been set yet — rough-in is inspected against outlets, trim against luminaires.
sections.figure_idea: A ceiling box labelled lighting outlet with the luminaire below it labelled as the complete unit, lamp to housing.

sections.title: Service — the family of service terms
sections.plain_explanation:
Article 100 splits 'service' into a family of terms, and the rules in Article 230 hang on the differences.
• Service: the conductors and equipment for delivering electric energy from the serving utility to the wiring system of the premises served.
• Service point: the point where the utility's facilities meet the premises wiring — the boundary of responsibility.
• Service conductors: the conductors from the service point to the service disconnecting means. Overhead, they divide into the service drop and the service-entrance conductors; underground, the utility's run is the service lateral.
• Service drop: the overhead conductors from the utility's system to the service point — the utility's side.
• Service-entrance conductors: on the customer's side, from the service point to the service equipment.
• Service equipment: the gear — usually the main disconnect, its overcurrent devices and their enclosure — that controls and cuts off the supply to the building.
sections.on_the_job: Find the service point first on any service change. It decides whose rules govern each run of conductor and where the grounded and grounding conductors are bonded together. On a 200 A upgrade in Ocala, Sharma's NEC work starts at the service point: the meter sits outside and the panel inside, back to back (S-09), with new Siemens service equipment, while the drop and the utility's side follow the serving utility's own requirements.
sections.sharma_note: S-09: meter outside and panel inside, back to back, where the house allows. The working-space rules of 110.26 still apply in full to that panel.
sections.figure_idea: One-line from utility pole through drop, meter and main disconnect into the panel, with service point, service conductors and service equipment labelled.
sections.florida_note: The utility serving the job (for example FPL or a municipal utility) sets its own service-point and meter requirements alongside the NEC. Confirm the utility's current requirements on service work.

sections.why_it_exists: Nearly every service argument is a service-point argument: whose conductor failed, whose standard applies, who pays for the repair. These definitions draw one line that everyone — utility, contractor, inspector — can point to, so responsibility is settled by the definitions instead of by whoever argues longest.
inspection_fails: Service point never confirmed with the utility: the crew built to the wrong side of the boundary and the utility refused the connection.
Grounded and grounding conductors bonded in a subpanel instead of at the service equipment — the main bonding jumper landed in the wrong place.
Service disconnect not at the nearest point of entrance of the service-entrance conductors (230.70(A)(1)) — a long unfused run inside the building.
Meter arrangement built to the NEC but not to the serving utility's requirements; the utility's side carries its own standards.
sections.exam_trap: The trap is calling everything from the pole to the panel 'the service drop.' The drop is only the utility's overhead run, and it ends at the service point. The customer's overhead conductors from the service point to the service equipment are service-entrance conductors — a different term, a different owner, and different rules.

sections.title: Service conductors, drop, lateral, entrance, equipment, and point
sections.plain_explanation: The service family, piece by piece. The service point is the point where the utility's facilities meet the premises wiring — the boundary of responsibility. Service conductors run from the service point to the service disconnecting means. Overhead, they split into the service drop (the utility's overhead conductors from its system to the service point) and service-entrance conductors (on the customer side, from the service point to the service equipment). Underground, the utility's run to the service point is the service lateral. Service equipment is the gear — usually the main disconnect and its enclosure — that controls and cuts off the supply to the building. The base Service page introduces the family; this page is the map of who owns what, where.
sections.on_the_job: Nearly every service argument is a service-point argument: whose conductor, whose repair, whose standard. On Sharma services the meter sits outside and the panel inside, back to back, so the service-entrance run stays as short as the layout allows — and the utility's requirements govern everything on its side of the point.
sections.sharma_note: S-09: meter outside and panel inside, back to back, where the layout allows — the arrangement that keeps the service-entrance conductors short.

sections.title: In sight from — and disconnecting means
sections.plain_explanation: Two linked terms. A disconnecting means is the device, or group of devices, that disconnects a circuit's conductors from their supply — a breaker or a disconnect switch are the everyday examples. Equipment is in sight from other equipment when it is visible from it and not more than 50 ft away; both halves matter, so a disconnect 20 ft away but hidden behind a wall is not in sight. Many equipment articles require a disconnect to be in sight from the equipment it serves, or to be lockable where they allow it to be out of sight.
sections.on_the_job: When you set a condenser or air-handler disconnect, stand at the equipment and look: if you cannot see the disconnect, or it is beyond 50 ft, the in-sight option is not met and the lockable route or a relocation is the conversation to have before trim-out.
sections.figure_idea: A condenser with a sight line drawn to its disconnect on the wall 15 ft away marked in sight, and a second disconnect drawn behind a fence marked not in sight.

sections.title: Device, disconnecting means, and switch types
sections.plain_explanation: A device is a unit of an electrical system, other than a conductor, that carries or controls electric energy — switches, receptacles, breakers and thermostats are devices; wire and conduit are not. A disconnecting means is a device, group of devices, or other means by which the conductors of a circuit can be disconnected from their source — the thing the In Sight page measures from. Three switch types round out the family: a general-use switch controls lighting and appliance loads and is rated in amperes at its marked voltage; an isolating switch is meant to isolate a circuit from its source and is not intended to interrupt current under load; a motor-circuit switch is rated in horsepower and is built to interrupt the maximum operating overload current of the motor it serves.
sections.on_the_job: An isolating switch is not a load-break switch — opening one under load is an arc event, not a disconnect. When a rule calls for a disconnecting means, check that the device in hand is actually rated to do the disconnecting job for that load type.
sections.figure_idea: Three switches in a row — general-use, isolating, motor-circuit — with the load each is built to interrupt drawn beside it.

sections.title: Premises wiring, separately derived systems, raceway, and splices
sections.plain_explanation: The premises wiring system is all the wiring inside (and attached to) a building, from the service point — or from another power source such as a generator or solar system — out to the outlets; it does not include the internal wiring of equipment itself. A separately derived system is a premises wiring system fed from a source other than a service — a transformer, generator, converter or battery — that has no direct electrical connection to the supply conductors of another system, other than through grounding and bonding. A raceway is an enclosed channel built to hold conductors or cables — conduit and tubing are raceways; cable is not. A splice is the connection between conductors, and a splicing wire connector is the device — wire nut, lever connector, terminal block — listed to make that connection under pressure. A hoistway is the shaft-like space an elevator, dumbwaiter or similar equipment travels in, a space with its own wiring rules in Article 620.
sections.on_the_job: A transformer-fed panel is a separately derived system, which is why it gets its own neutral-to-ground bond through a system bonding jumper — the bond the Grounding family page describes. And every splice a crew makes lives or dies by the connector's listing: the connector, not the tape over it, is the splice.
sections.figure_idea: A building outline from service point to last outlet labelled premises wiring, a transformer feeding its own panel labelled separately derived, and a raceway cut open to show the conductors inside.

sections.title: Special permission
sections.plain_explanation:
Special permission is the written consent of the AHJ, given where the Code says the AHJ may allow an alternative. It is not a verbal okay from a plans examiner, a builder or a homeowner, and it is not something an electrician grants himself. Where the Code requires it, get it in writing before the work is done.
• Written — if it is not on paper, it is not special permission.
• From the AHJ — the authority enforcing the Code on that job (90.4), not the builder, the owner or the supply house.
• Before the work — consent chased after the fact is an argument, not a permission.
• Only where the Code contemplates it — the AHJ grants special permission where the rules allow it; the rest of the rules have no such door.
sections.on_the_job: If a job depends on special permission, paper it: keep the AHJ's written consent with the permit documents so the next inspector sees the same record. A note in the job file saying 'the inspector was fine with it' is not the consent — get the signed approval itself, and file it where the final inspector will find it.
sections.why_it_exists: The written rule protects everybody on the job. The next inspector sees the same record the first one agreed to, the contractor is not caught between a verbal yes and a written no, and an alternative method gets one accountable decision instead of a hallway conversation nobody can prove later.
sections.exam_trap: The trap answer treats a verbal okay — from a plans examiner, an inspector, or the builder — as special permission. The definition is narrower: the written consent of the AHJ. No writing, no permission, however senior the person who nodded.
inspection_fails: Alternative method built on a verbal okay; the final inspector has no record of it and writes it up.
Work done first, written consent requested after — the AHJ declines, and the work comes out.
Builder's letter filed as 'special permission' — the consent never came from the AHJ.
Consent letter left at the office; nothing with the permit documents on site when the inspector asks.

sections.title: Garage, kitchen, and laundry area — how the Code uses area names
sections.plain_explanation: Of these three area names, only one is a formal Article 100 definition: a kitchen is "an area with a sink and permanent provisions for food preparation and cooking" — both halves must be present, and a portable appliance plugged in on the counter does not create one. Garage and laundry area carry no standalone Article 100 definition in the 2020 Code. The Code uses both terms in its rules — garage receptacles and their GFCI protection in 210.8(A)(2) and 210.52(G), the laundry area branch circuit in 210.11(C)(2) and laundry-area GFCI in 210.8(A)(10) — and they take their ordinary meaning: the garage is the vehicle space and its attached unfinished areas, and the laundry area is where laundry equipment is installed or intended to be. So treat the kitchen test as a definition to apply exactly, and the other two as usage terms settled by the plan's intended use of the space.
sections.on_the_job: When a plan is vague about a room's use, settle it before rough-in — a laundry area moved after wiring changes GFCI protection and circuit requirements. The detailed area rules live in Article 210 and are covered in Chapter 2 of this book.

sections.title: Article 110 — Requirements for electrical installations
sections.plain_explanation:
Article 110 sets the general rules that apply to almost every installation: use approved and listed equipment the way its listing intends, terminate conductors correctly, do neat and workmanlike work, mark what needs marking, and leave safe working space around equipment. If a habit is wrong on every job, the rule against it is probably in this article.
• Approval and listing: equipment is approved (110.2) and installed and used the way its listing and labeling intend (110.3(B)). A breaker that merely fits the slot is not approved for the panel.
• Terminations: conductors land on terminals rated for the metal and tightened to the marking (110.14).
• Workmanship: neat and workmanlike, with covers and deadfronts in place (110.12).
• Working space: clear space in front of equipment that may be worked on energized — 3 ft deep at a 120/240 V house panel (110.26(A)).
• Identification: disconnecting means marked to show what they disconnect (110.22).
sections.on_the_job: Most Article 110 failures are visible without a meter: wrong-brand breakers, sloppy terminations, unmarked disconnects, blocked panels. A slow walk with this article in mind catches them before the inspector does. On a Sharma final walk in Marion Oaks that means Siemens breakers in the Siemens panel (new gear is Siemens), every disconnect labeled, and the 3 ft in front of the panel swept clear of the builder's paint cans before the inspector arrives.

They come from the basics that show up on every job: a loose lug heating for years, a wrong-brand breaker that was never tested in that panel, a panel nobody can reach in an emergency. Article 110 is where the Code parks those basics, which is why inspectors write it up more than almost anything else.

sections.title: Scope of Article 110
sections.plain_explanation:
Article 110 states the general requirements for electrical installations. It is the Code's ground floor: before any equipment article or wiring-method article adds its own rules, Article 110 sets the terms every installation has to meet.
• Approval and examination: equipment is approved (110.2), examined for suitability (110.3), and listed gear is installed and used by its instructions (110.3(B)).
• Ratings and fault duty: equipment is used at the voltage it is rated for (110.4), and its interrupting and short-circuit ratings have to suit the system (110.9, 110.10).
• Connections: conductors land on terminals suited to them, tightened to the specified torque (110.14, 110.14(D)).
• Marking and space: equipment is durably marked with its ratings (110.21), and access and working space are provided and kept clear around it (110.26).
• Two voltage worlds: Part II covers installations of 1000 volts, nominal, or less. Part III adds stricter rules for installations over 1000 volts (110.31).
The article is not limited to services or to panels. It follows equipment into every occupancy the later articles cover — houses, stores, factories, hospitals — and the specific articles then add their own rules on top of these. They do not replace them.
sections.on_the_job: On a Marion Oaks new home, three rough-in questions are Article 110 questions, not house-article questions. Is the panel's interrupting rating enough for the fault current the utility can deliver (110.9)? Are the lugs torqued to the value printed on the panel label (110.14(D))? Is the working space — 30 in wide, 3 ft deep — taped out and kept clear in the garage (110.26(A))? Start in 110, then open the equipment's own article for whatever it adds.

sections.why_it_exists: Most electrical failures are not exotic. A loose termination, gear used outside its rating, a panel nobody can stand in front of — the same short list starts fires and hurts people in houses and factories alike. Article 110 exists so those basics are required once, everywhere, instead of being re-argued occupancy by occupancy.

sections.exam_trap: The trap is treating Article 110 as 'the service article' or 'the panel article' and skipping it on equipment questions. Its scope is every installation: a motor, a luminaire or a disconnect can be failed on an Article 110 rule — suitability, torque, working space — underneath its own article's rules.
