sections.title: Approval of equipment and conductors
sections.plain_explanation:
Conductors and equipment required or permitted by the Code are acceptable only if approved. Approved is an Article 100 word: it means acceptable to the authority having jurisdiction. In practice, approval is shown through listing and labeling by a qualified testing laboratory, and the four words of the family are not interchangeable:
• Approved — acceptable to the AHJ.
• Listed — the product appears in the testing organization's published list of products it has evaluated.
• Labeled — the testing organization has attached its label to the product.
• Identified — recognizable as suitable for the specific use in question.
Equipment with no path to approval does not become acceptable because it was cheap, available, or already on the truck. A product can be well made and still not be listed, and a breaker that physically fits a foreign panel is not thereby identified for that panel.
sections.on_the_job: Check approvals at order and delivery time, not at trim-out. The breaker question is settled before the truck rolls: Siemens gear for new work (S-02), and in an existing panel only the breakers listed for that panel — a Square D panel gets Square D breakers (S-03), even when another brand snaps in and 'works.' A non-listed substitute discovered at trim-out costs a return trip and can hold up the whole job.
sections.sharma_note: S-02 and S-03 keep Sharma inside this rule: Siemens gear for new work, and only breakers listed for the panel in existing panels.

sections.why_it_exists: Listing is the evidence that a product was tested against the hazards it will meet — heat, fault current, flame, and how it behaves when it fails. Unapproved gear has no evaluated failure story, so when it lets go, it lets go as a surprise: the breaker that never trips, the driver that cooks in a closed ceiling. AHJ acceptance is also the practical gate to a passed inspection and an energized building.

Equipment in service with its listing label removed or unreadable, so approval cannot be verified (110.2).

Approval is acceptance by the AHJ, normally proven by listing and labeling, and identified is use-specific: the same breaker can be listed as a product and still not be identified for the panel it was forced into.

sections.title: Examination, identification, installation, and use of equipment
sections.plain_explanation:
110.3(A) lists what is weighed when equipment is examined and judged for an installation:
• Suitability for the installation and use.
• Mechanical strength and durability.
• Wire-bending space and connection space for its conductors.
• Electrical insulation.
• Heating effects.
• Arcing effects.
• Classification by type, size, voltage, current capacity and specific use.
In plain terms: the right equipment, of the right rating, in the right place, with room for its conductors to land properly. 110.3(B) then requires listed or labeled equipment to be installed and used in accordance with its instructions, and 110.3(C) covers listing of equipment by a qualified electrical testing laboratory where the Code requires it. Suitability is judged before the gear goes in — not after the inspector arrives.
sections.on_the_job: Suitability is decided before installation. On a Lake County pool job, the replacement pump motor that came out of the box was an open drip-proof motor meant for a dry location; the equipment pad sits out in the weather beside the pool. sections.title: Install and use listed equipment per its instructions
sections.plain_explanation:
Listed or labeled equipment must be installed and used in accordance with the instructions included in its listing or labeling. The manufacturer's instructions are not suggestions where the listing depends on them:
• A torque value in the instructions is a requirement. 110.14(D) sends you back to it, with a torque tool in hand.
• A conductor-material marking — copper only, or CU-AL — limits what may land on the terminal.
• A temperature marking works with the termination rules of 110.14(C): sizing starts from the 60 °C column, or the 75 °C column where the equipment is listed and marked for it.
• A mounting requirement — orientation, clearance, enclosure type — is part of the listing, not a preference.
If the instructions and a habit disagree, the instructions win.
sections.on_the_job: On a Marion Oaks trim-out, the door label of the Siemens panel gives the lug torque table and marks the terminations 75 °C. The apprentice torques the feeder lugs to the printed value with a torque wrench and lands the conductors the label allows. The same panel closed up 'hand tight by feel' is the call-back Sharma takes six months later: a hot lug and a nuisance-tripped main. Read the label inside the panel door, the sheet in the device box, and the nameplate on the equipment. If the instructions and a habit disagree, the instructions win.

sections.title: Voltages
sections.plain_explanation:
The voltage considered is the voltage at which the circuit operates, and equipment's voltage rating may not be less than the nominal voltage of the circuit it is connected to. Equipment is used at the voltage it is rated for, and where the Code states a voltage it means the nominal system voltage the circuit actually operates at, unless a rule says otherwise. A device rated for a lower voltage does not become suitable on a higher-voltage circuit because its terminals fit, and the nominal voltage is what load, protection and clearance rules are keyed to.

Common nominal system voltages (the list itself is in 220.5(A), not 110.4):
• 120 V — single-phase branch circuits
• 120/240 V — the standard one-family house service
• 208Y/120 V — three-phase wye, common in commercial buildings and multifamily services
• 240 V — single-phase or three-phase delta
• 277 V — one leg of a 480Y/277 V system to neutral, the commercial lighting voltage
• 480Y/277 V and 480 V — larger commercial services
Equipment is rated for the nominal voltage of the system it is connected to; a device marked for one system voltage is not interchangeable with another just because the plugs look alike.
sections.on_the_job: Check the nameplate voltage against the system in front of you — 120/240 single-phase, 208Y/120 and 480Y/277 three-phase are different worlds for device ratings even when the hardware looks similar.

sections.title: Conductors — general
sections.plain_explanation:
Conductors in the Code are copper unless a rule or an equipment marking provides for another metal. Where other materials such as aluminum or copper-clad aluminum are used, the sizes in the Code's tables and rules are read in the column and on the terms for that material. The metal of the conductor is part of the design, not an afterthought at the supply house.
• Table 310.16 has two column families: copper on the left; aluminum and copper-clad aluminum sharing the right-hand columns.
• Same size, different metal, different answer: 12 AWG at 75 °C is 25 A in copper and 20 A in aluminum or CCA.
• The breaker caps follow the metal too (240.4(D)): 12 AWG copper is capped at 20 A; 12 AWG aluminum or CCA at 15 A.
• Terminations must be marked for the metal landed on them (110.14).
sections.on_the_job: Service change on a Marion Oaks house: the underground lateral is aluminum, the branch circuits are copper, and each metal gets read in its own column before anything is ordered. Where CCA goes in on a Sharma house, S-10 sets the pattern — one AWG size larger than the copper it replaces: 12 AWG CCA on a 15 A circuit, 10 AWG CCA on a 20 A circuit, landed only on terminations marked for it and never backstabbed. If the spool on the truck is not the metal the takeoff assumed, the sizing starts over.
sections.sharma_note: S-10: copper is Sharma's default. When CCA is used, size one AWG larger, use the aluminum column of Table 310.16, land it only on terminations listed for it, and never backstab.

sections.title: Conductor sizes — AWG and circular mils
sections.plain_explanation:
Conductor sizes are expressed in American Wire Gauge for the smaller sizes and in circular mil area for the larger ones. The size designation is a standard language: the same AWG number means the same conductor size whoever made the cable. Size by itself is not ampacity — the rating still comes from the ampacity tables, the termination limits and the conditions of use.

Circular-mil areas for the sizes Sharma pulls most (above 4/0, the kcmil number is the area in thousands of circular mils):
• 14 AWG — 4,110 circular mils
• 12 AWG — 6,530 circular mils
• 10 AWG — 10,380 circular mils
• 8 AWG — 16,510 circular mils
• 6 AWG — 26,240 circular mils
• 4 AWG — 41,740 circular mils
• 2 AWG — 66,360 circular mils
• 1/0 AWG — 105,600 circular mils
• 2/0 AWG — 133,100 circular mils
• 3/0 AWG — 167,800 circular mils
• 4/0 AWG — 211,600 circular mils
These areas are what the proportional upsizing rules work from — when conductors are upsized, grounding conductors are upsized by the ratio of these numbers (see 250.122 in Chapter 2).
sections.on_the_job: Speak sizes in AWG up through 4/0 and in kcmil above that, and never let a breaker handle rating substitute for the ampacity check behind it.

sections.title: Wiring integrity
sections.plain_explanation:
Completed wiring installations must be free from three things:
• Short circuits — conductors touching that should never touch.
• Ground faults — a live conductor connected to ground or to grounded metal by a path that is not supposed to exist.
• Any connection to ground other than the ones the Code requires or permits — the grounded conductor meets ground where the Code says, and nowhere else.
That is the whole rule of 110.7, and it is why continuity and insulation checks happen before energizing: the installation has to be proven clean, not assumed clean. Do not confuse it with equipment integrity. The rule that internal parts, busbars, wiring terminals, and other parts must not be damaged or contaminated lives at 110.12(B), not here. Section 110.7 is about the wiring; 110.12(B) is about the gear.
sections.on_the_job: Before you energize, prove the install: no shorts, no ground faults, no stray grounds. On a final check at an Ocala house, our continuity test caught a dead short on a 20 A kitchen circuit before the panel was ever made hot — a drywall screw had pierced the run behind the cabinets. Twenty minutes with the meter; the same fault found after energizing would have meant a tripping breaker, a callback, and a finished wall opened on warranty. If the gear itself is damaged or contaminated inside, that is a 110.12(B) problem — a different section, with the same stop-and-fix answer.
sections.why_it_exists: A short or a ground fault that nobody finds on test day gets found by the breaker, by an arc, or by the person who touches the metal — at full fault current, with the building occupied. Testing before energizing is the cheap moment to catch a nicked conductor or a stray ground connection. After energizing, the same defect is a fire investigation or a shock injury.
sections.exam_trap: The exam trap is 110.12(B) dressed as 110.7. A question describes damaged busbars or contaminated internal parts and offers 110.7 as the answer — wrong section; that is equipment integrity at 110.12(B). Section 110.7 covers the completed wiring only: free from short circuits, ground faults, and connections to ground that the Code does not require or permit.

sections.title: Wiring methods — use only recognized methods
sections.plain_explanation:
Only wiring methods the Code recognizes for the application may be used. A cable or raceway that conducts electricity is not thereby a permitted wiring method for a given location: each method has its own article, its permitted uses and its prohibited uses, and those govern.
• NM cable — Article 334. EMT — Article 358. PVC conduit — Article 352. MC cable — Article 330. AC cable — Article 320. Rigid metal conduit — Article 344.
• The article's limits decide the locations: indoors, outdoors, wet, concealed, exposed.
• Improvised assemblies and products used outside their article's limits fail here before any other rule is reached.
sections.on_the_job: Before running anything, name the method and its article — NM cable, EMT, PVC, MC and the rest each carry their own use lists. A method allowed indoors is not automatically allowed outdoors or in a wet location. On a detached-garage feed in Clermont, that means the decision happens before the material list: NM inside the house walls, a method whose article permits the underground run, and a method permitted exposed on the garage's block wall. Name the method first and the rough-in survives inspection.

That reaches wiring outside buildings too. A recognized wiring method can go in any type of building, occupancy or premises wiring system, unless another rule says otherwise.

sections.title: Interrupting rating
sections.plain_explanation:
Equipment meant to interrupt current during a fault has to be able to interrupt the fault current that can actually be delivered at its terminals. A breaker asked to open a fault beyond its interrupting rating can fail violently instead of clearing the fault. The rating is printed on the device and must equal or exceed the available fault current at that point.
Two companion rules travel with it:
• 110.10: the whole circuit — overcurrent devices, total impedance and the short-circuit current ratings of the components — must work together so a fault clears without extensive damage.
• 110.24: at service equipment in other than dwelling units, the available fault current is field-marked on the equipment, with the date the calculation was made.
sections.on_the_job: Check the kAIC marking on breakers against the job's available fault current, especially close to large services and transformers. Worked example from a small commercial service: the fault-current calculation comes back at 22 kA. A panel filled with 10 kAIC breakers is under-rated gear — every one of those breakers is being asked to open a fault more than twice its rating. Breakers marked 22 kAIC meet the number exactly; 65 kAIC gear covers it with room for the utility's next transformer change. Series-rated combinations are only valid as tested and documented combinations, not as a field guess. Sharma standard is Siemens on new gear — read the kAIC on the label before the gear is set, not at trim-out.

nec2023_change.change: A wording update using the defined term available fault current. Every breaker and fuse still has to be rated to interrupt the available fault current at its line terminals. Any breaker or fuse meant to open fault current needs an interrupting rating that meets or beats the available fault current at its line terminals.

sections.why_it_exists: A breaker that tries to open a fault beyond its rating can weld its contacts, rupture, or keep feeding the arc — the fault burns on instead of clearing. And available fault current is not fixed: when the utility swaps in a bigger transformer, the same panel can become under-rated without anyone on site touching it.

Replacement breaker of a different type with a lower interrupting rating swapped in during a repair.

The interrupting rating is the kAIC number, and a little 20 A breaker can carry 65 kAIC while a big frame breaker carries only 10 kAIC.

sections.title: Circuit impedance and fault-current performance
sections.plain_explanation:
110.10 is the performance rule standing behind the rating rules. The overcurrent devices, the total impedance of the circuit, and the other components of the circuit must be selected and coordinated so that, under a short circuit or ground fault, the fault is cleared without extensive damage to the equipment in the circuit.
• The fault loop has to be a low-impedance path: conductors, raceway, bonding and grounding connections tight enough that a fault draws current high enough to open the device fast. A high-impedance loop can leave a fault arcing at a current too low to trip anything.
• Every device that has to open the fault needs an interrupting rating at least equal to the available fault current at its terminals (110.9).
• Every component in the circuit needs a short-circuit current rating that suits the system it is part of — it can only be asked to withstand the fault energy the circuit can actually deliver.
No single part passes or fails alone. 110.10 judges the circuit as a team.
sections.on_the_job: Small commercial tenant build-out in Ocala: the utility's fault-current letter for the new 400 A service states an available fault current of 22,000 A. The specified Siemens panelboard carries a 22 kA short-circuit current rating and its breakers are rated 22 kA interrupting, so the team matches the system. The value-brand panel the GC tried to substitute was marked 10 kA; under 110.9 and 110.10 it cannot go in, however good the price. The available fault current is field-marked on the service equipment with the date the calculation was made (110.24).

sections.why_it_exists: A fault is the highest-energy event a circuit ever sees. If the loop impedance is too high, the breaker never trips and the fault burns until something melts open. If a component's rating is too low, it can rupture instead of opening. The rule exists so a fault ends as a trip — not a fire, and not an explosion.
inspection_fails: Breakers with an interrupting rating below the available fault current at their line terminals (110.9, 110.10).

Available fault current not field-marked at the service, or the marking left stale after a utility change raised it (110.24).
sections.exam_trap: The trap answer: 'the breaker is rated 22 kA, so the installation complies.' 110.10 is wider than any one device. A correctly rated breaker on a high-impedance fault loop still fails the section, because the fault never clears — impedance and every component's withstand rating count too.

sections.title: Deteriorating agents
sections.plain_explanation:
Equipment must not sit in conditions that will destroy it. Unless equipment is identified for the operating environment, it does not go where it will be exposed to:
• Damp or wet locations.
• Gases, fumes, vapors, liquids, or other agents that have a deteriorating effect on the equipment or the conductors.
• Excessive temperatures.
Ordinary equipment in a corrosive or wet environment fails early, and it can fail dangerously. The answer is not paint or tape; the answer is equipment identified for that environment, which in practice means the enclosure type marked on the gear. The types Sharma meets most, from 110.28:
• Type 1 — indoor, general purpose.
• Type 3R — outdoor and rainproof; the standard house disconnect and meter enclosure.
• Type 4 — watertight, even against hose-directed water.
• Type 4X — Type 4 performance plus corrosion resistance, for washdown and coastal work.
• Type 12 — indoor industrial, against dust and dripping noncorrosive liquids.
sections.on_the_job: Coastal Florida is the standing test case. On a service call at a beachside house in Brevard County, the disconnect on the ocean-side wall was rusted through at the bottom seam after a few salt-air seasons, with green corrosion on the lugs. That is a replacement, not a cleanup: Type 3R minimum outside, and Type 4X where hose water or pool chemicals join the salt. In the pool equipment room at the same house, chlorine stored beside the panel had done the same work through the air. Identify the environment first, then pick equipment identified for it.
sections.florida_note: Salt air along Florida coasts is a deteriorating agent. Exterior and coastal gear needs to be identified for the exposure, and corrosion found at service calls should be reported, not just wiped off.

sections.why_it_exists: Corrosion does not stop at the cabinet skin. It eats lugs and terminations, raises resistance at every joint, and turns a sound connection into a heater. Moisture and chemical vapor work the same way from the inside, attacking insulation and bus. Gear that rots in place fails years early, and the failure is usually heat or a ground fault, not a clean shutdown.
inspection_fails: Indoor Type 1 panel or disconnect mounted on an exterior coastal wall, rusted at the seams and terminations (110.11).
Ordinary disconnect in a pool equipment room with chlorine stored in the same room; corroded enclosure and lugs (110.11).
Standard indoor equipment in a fertilizer storage room or a car wash bay, attacked by chemical vapor and hose-directed water (110.11).
Equipment mounted where excessive temperatures were never accounted for, with no check that it is identified for the heat (110.11).
sections.exam_trap: The trap is treating identification as a coating: spray it with rust-proof paint and call it identified for the coast. Identification is the manufacturer's rating, shown by the type marked on the enclosure. Paint does not turn a Type 1 box into a Type 4X, and a stainless look does not either. If the marked type does not cover the exposure, the equipment does not belong there.

sections.title: Mechanical execution of work — workmanship and unused openings
sections.plain_explanation:
Electrical work has to be done in a neat and workmanlike manner. Unused openings in enclosures, boxes and equipment have to be closed with closures that give protection much like the wall of the equipment itself — a missing knockout blank is an open door for fingers, pests and arc products. Conductors must also be protected where insulation can be damaged. (Keeping water out of enclosures in wet locations is a different rule — see 312.2 and 314.15 — not part of 110.12.) Part (B) covers integrity of equipment and connections: internal parts, busbars, wiring terminals, and other components must not be damaged or contaminated by foreign materials, and there must be no damaged, broken, bent, cut, or deteriorated parts.

NEC 2023 CHANGE:
• 110.12: Neat and workmanlike is out. The standard for every electrical install is now professional and skillful work. The workmanship standard changed from neat and workmanlike to professional and skillful.
FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.
sections.on_the_job: Close every unused opening with a listed blank or plug, not tape or a folded piece of can. Neat work is not cosmetic here — it is the section the inspector cites when a panel looks like a hazard even before testing anything.

sections.florida_note: Open knockouts in exterior Florida enclosures are also a pest and water entry. Close them the same day the gear is set.

sections.title: Mounting and cooling of equipment
sections.plain_explanation:
Equipment has to be firmly secured to its mounting surface, and it must not be mounted in a way that blocks the cooling it was designed for. Section 110.13 states the two duties separately:
• Mounting — 110.13(A): equipment must be firmly secured to the mounting surface. Wooden plugs driven into masonry, concrete or plaster are not an acceptable way to secure equipment.
• Cooling — 110.13(B): equipment that depends on the natural circulation of air must not be installed so the airflow over its cooling surfaces is prevented. It cannot be buried in insulation or boxed in tight.
Where the manufacturer's instructions set spacing the equipment needs to breathe, those instructions carry Code force through 110.3(B).
sections.on_the_job: Anchor gear with real fasteners into structure or masonry anchors, keep vents and fins clear, and check that a recessed installation still lets the equipment breathe as its instructions require. On a block garage wall that means sleeve or wedge anchors into the block — never a wooden plug — and no boxes stored against a dry-type transformer's fins.
sections.why_it_exists: Loose gear vibrates, works its terminations loose, and can pull against its raceways. Overheated gear cooks its insulation and electronics and fails years early — or becomes the ignition source itself. Florida garages and attics run hot to begin with, so the cooling margin the manufacturer designed in is not spare capacity to spend on storage and insulation.
sections.exam_trap: Two traps live on this page. A wooden plug in a masonry wall can feel solid, so it must be fine — 110.13(A) names it as not permitted for securing equipment. And equipment that physically fits in a tight box must be allowed to run in one — if it cools by natural air circulation, boxing it in defeats the design and fails 110.13(B).
inspection_fails: Transformer hung on wooden plugs in a block wall — 110.13(A) names the method as not permitted.
Insulation blown over and around a recessed unit until its vents are buried.
Storage stacked tight against a dry-type transformer's fins; the unit runs hot to the touch.
Equipment loose on its anchors, rocking when the raceway is pulled.

sections.title: Electrical connections — terminations in general
sections.plain_explanation:
Most electrical failures start at a connection, and this section is the Code's main defense. Conductors must land on terminals suited to their metal and size, with the connection made by an approved method. Dissimilar metals in contact must be handled only where the device is identified for that combination, because corrosion between unlike metals loosens and overheats a joint over time. Solder, where used, cannot be the thing that holds a joint against pulling apart.

NEC 2023 CHANGE:
• 110.14: Terminals now have to make a mechanically secure electrical connection, replacing the old thoroughly good wording, and the example metal pairs were cut from the dissimilar-metals rule. 110.14(A): landing a conductor on a terminal has to produce a mechanically secure electrical connection, with no damage to the wire.
FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.
sections.on_the_job: Read the lug and device markings before landing wire. CU-only means copper only. A connector for aluminum, copper and CCA together must carry the AL-CU or CU-AL marking, or the intermixed marking where the metals actually touch, and breaker and equipment lugs get the same check.
sections.sharma_note: S-10 CCA practice: 15A and 20A device screw terminals take copper and CCA unless marked otherwise; devices 30A and up are copper-only unless marked AL/CU. Copper and CCA are not dissimilar metals; aluminum with copper, or aluminum with CCA, is. Backstab (push-in) terminals are 14 AWG solid copper only — never backstab CCA, stranded wire, or 12 AWG. UNVERIFIED FLAG (v1 README item 9): the UL guide wording behind the CCA terminal markings (RTRT / WJQR / ZMVV / AALZ) was taken from NEMA and UL/IAEI quotations, not read first-hand in UL Product iQ, and no CC or CC/CU marking was found in the ZMVV table. Do not invent a marking. A NEMA citation to 404.15(C) for switch terminals was not checked against the code text and is not relied on here.

sections.title: Temperature limits at terminations
sections.plain_explanation: A conductor's ampacity may be read from a higher temperature column only if the terminations at both ends are rated for that temperature. For circuits of 100A or less, or using 14 through 1 AWG conductors, the default is the 60 degree C column unless the equipment is marked otherwise. For larger circuits the default is the 75 degree C column. The temperature rating of a conductor cannot be used above the lowest temperature rating of any termination it lands on.
sections.on_the_job: This is why 90 degree wire still gets sized from the 60 or 75 degree column at the breaker. Read the breaker and equipment markings; existing v1 item L-033 works the 110.14(C)(1) case in detail.
sections.figure_idea: A conductor run drawn as a chain — wire rated 90, breaker lug rated 75, equipment lug rated 60 — with the whole chain sized at the weakest link, 60.

sections.title: Torque — tighten to the specified value
sections.plain_explanation:
Where a manufacturer gives a torque value for a terminal, the connection has to be tightened to that value using an approved means, unless the equipment has been tested and marked so another method is known to give the same result.
• The approved means is a calibrated torque tool — a torque wrench or torque screwdriver — or a device such as a shear bolt or breakaway fastener that shows the proper torque was reached.
• The specified torque is normally printed on the equipment label or in its instructions. Those instructions carry Code force under 110.3(B).
• Hand-tight by feel is not a value. Two installers' 'tight' can differ by half.
• If no value is indicated, contact the manufacturer. In the absence of a manufacturer's value, Annex I of UL 486A-486B — reprinted as NEC Informative Annex I — gives torque values by screw and conductor size.
sections.on_the_job: New 200 A Siemens panel on a slab home in Ocala: the torque table is printed on the label inside the door — main lugs, neutral bar and breaker terminals each carry their own value. The torque screwdriver handles the small breaker and device terminals; the main lugs take a torque wrench. Keep both on the truck, use the label value for every lug at trim and service work, and re-check after landing all conductors — a lug torqued before the last conductor went in is not finished. Existing checklist item SP-15 covers the field routine.
sections.figure_idea: Torque screwdriver on a breaker lug with the panel label's torque table beside it.

sections.why_it_exists: A loose terminal is a resistor. Current through a high-resistance joint makes heat, the heat cycles loosen the joint further, and the end of that road is arcing, a burned lug, or a fire inside the panel. Too tight is its own failure: crushed strands, a cracked lug, or a screw that snaps later. The specified value is the one the equipment was tested at — that is why the Code makes it a rule instead of a suggestion.

Main lugs run down with an impact driver until the tool 'sounded right.'
Label torque table ignored; generic values used even though the manufacturer printed its own.
Conductor strands crushed and splayed from over-torque, lug cracked at the barrel.
sections.exam_trap: The trap answer is 'gudentight' — snug plus a quarter turn. 110.14(D) wants the indicated value, reached with an approved means. The second trap is reaching for the Annex I fallback values when the equipment label prints a value: the manufacturer's number governs, and the fallback exists only for when no value is given.

sections.title: High-leg marking on 4-wire delta systems
sections.plain_explanation:
On a 4-wire, 3-phase delta system where the midpoint of one phase winding is used as a circuit conductor — the common 240/120 V delta — the voltages to ground are not equal:
• Two legs sit at 120 V to ground.
• The third leg — the high leg — sits at 208 V to ground.
110.15 requires that high-leg conductor to be durably and permanently marked by an orange finish, or identified by other effective means, at each point on the system where a connection is made if the grounded conductor is also present. The marking is what keeps a 120 V load from being landed on the leg that sits at 208 V to ground.
sections.on_the_job: Sharma meets high legs on older light-commercial services. Before landing any 120 V circuit in a delta panel, identify which leg is the high leg, confirm it is orange-marked, and keep 120 V loads off it. On a panel change at a small warehouse, the crew meters every leg to ground before landing anything: A reads 120 V, B reads 208 V, C reads 120 V — B is the high leg. It gets its orange identification at the panel and at the disconnect, the 120 V lighting and receptacle circuits land on A and C only, and the panel schedule is marked so the next electrician sees it before he meters.
sections.figure_idea: A delta panel schedule with the B phase column shaded orange and the voltage-to-ground values 120 / 208 / 120 written under the three legs.
sections.why_it_exists: A 120 V load landed on the high leg sees 208 V to ground and burns up — controls, ballasts and electronics die, and equipment can be energized in ways nobody expects. A delta panel looks like any other panel from the front; the only thing standing between a tired apprentice and a fried control board is the orange identification on the odd leg. That is why the marking has to be durable and permanent, not a scrap of tape that falls off by trim-out.
sections.exam_trap: The trap answer marks the high leg with whatever tape is in the truck, or assumes a 120 V load can share the high leg because “it is still just one phase.” 110.15 requires an orange finish or other effective means, and the 208 V-to-ground leg feeds only loads rated for it.

sections.title: Arc-flash hazard warning marking
sections.plain_explanation:
Certain equipment that is likely to be examined, adjusted or worked on while energized — such as switchboards, panelboards and motor control centers in other than dwelling settings — must carry a durable field-applied warning marking telling people about the arc-flash hazard. The marking warns; it does not replace safe work practice, and it belongs where a person approaching the gear will see it. 110.16(B) (NEC 2020): in other than dwelling units, service equipment rated 1200A or more also needs a permanent label (meeting 110.21(B)) showing the nominal system voltage, the available fault current at the service overcurrent devices, the clearing time of those devices based on that fault current, and the date the label was applied; it is not required where an arc-flash label is applied per acceptable industry practice.

NEC 2023 CHANGE:
• 110.16(B): 110.16(B) now covers service equipment AND feeder-supplied equipment rated 1000A or more (was service equipment 1200A or more), and the permanent label must be an arc-flash label per applicable industry practice, with the date applied.
FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.
sections.on_the_job: On commercial work, confirm the arc-flash warning label is present and legible before final. Houses are not the target of this section, but the hazard it names is real on any energized panel.

sections.title: Servicing and maintenance of equipment
sections.plain_explanation:
This section is new in the 2023 NEC (it does not exist in NEC 2020, the edition Florida enforces), addresses the servicing and maintenance of electrical equipment: servicing is to be done by qualified persons, and replacement parts and components are to be suitable for the equipment — identified for it or the manufacturer's specified replacements. Experience alone is not the standard; the person doing the work needs the training and knowledge the task and its hazards require. The 2023 rule also says the work is done per the manufacturer's instructions or listing information, industry standards, or as approved by the AHJ, and replacement parts must be identified and come from the original manufacturer, be designed by an engineer experienced in replacement parts for that equipment, or be approved by the AHJ.

NEC 2023 CHANGE:
• 110.17: New section: only qualified, trained persons can service and maintain electrical equipment, and replacement parts have to be identified and verified to product standards. Only qualified persons, trained in servicing and maintaining equipment, can do that work.
FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.
sections.on_the_job: On service calls, replace failed components with parts identified for that equipment, and treat unfamiliar gear — especially commercial switchgear — as a qualified-persons-only job until the right person is on it.
sections.florida_note: Not in force on Florida jobs under NEC 2020 (permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026); know it for the NEC 2023 exam. FBC 9th Ed. (NEC 2023) applies to permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026.

sections.title: Arcing parts
sections.plain_explanation:
Some parts of electrical equipment arc in normal operation. Switch and breaker contacts open under load, contactors pull in and drop out, motor brushes ride a commutator — arcs, sparks, and sometimes molten metal are part of how the equipment works. 110.18 does not try to ban the arc. It controls where the arc may happen:
• Parts that in ordinary operation produce arcs, sparks, flames, or molten metal must be enclosed, or separated and isolated from all combustible material.
• An arc inside properly enclosed equipment is expected, and contained.
• The same arcing part sitting open near material that can ignite is a fire waiting for its fuel.
There is no distance in inches in this section. The test is a condition: enclosed, or separated and isolated.
sections.on_the_job: On a service call in a Marion Oaks garage, the pattern is familiar: a contactor or an old open switch with its cover long gone, cycling a load, with paint cans and cardboard stacked against the same wall. Keep enclosures intact around switching equipment. Put the cover back or replace the device, move the storage off the gear, and flag arcing or sparking equipment found open or mounted tight against combustible storage for correction before you leave.

sections.why_it_exists: Every switching operation throws a small, very hot plasma event. Inside an enclosure it dies against metal. In the open — next to cardboard, paint, solvents, or stored household goods — it is an ignition source that fires on a schedule, every time the equipment cycles. Florida garages and storage rooms put the fuel and the arcing parts within the same few feet, which is exactly the pairing this rule breaks up.

Open arcing equipment mounted tight against combustible storage, with no separation or isolation (110.18).
Brush-type motor run open next to hay, straw, or feed storage in a barn (110.18).
Damaged enclosure left in service so the arcing parts inside are no longer enclosed (110.18).
sections.exam_trap: The trap is hunting for a number: 'how many inches from combustibles does 110.18 require?' It gives none — the rule is a condition, not a dimension. The second trap is calling arcing parts defects by themselves. They are normal in switching equipment; the violation is leaving them open to fuel, not the arc itself.

sections.title: Light and power from railway conductors (orientation)
sections.plain_explanation:
110.19 draws one hard line: circuits for lighting and power shall not be connected to any system that contains trolley wires with a ground return.
• The ban is on the connection itself, not on the voltage. A ground-return trolley system carries its return current through the rails and the earth, and a building's lighting and power circuits must never be tied into that.
• One exception: the connection is permitted in car houses, power houses, and passenger and freight stations operated in connection with electric railways — the railway's own buildings, run by the railway.
• Nothing else in premises wiring uses this section. Railway power installations themselves sit largely outside the Code's scope (90.2). The page is in the book so the numbering of Article 110 reads complete, not as a working rule.
sections.on_the_job: Sharma does not design or install railway power, so the field case is a request, not an installation: on a commercial job near a rail corridor, someone proposes feeding site lighting or a temporary circuit from 'railway power' because it is close. The answer is the one this page exists for — stop and escalate. Temporary power comes from the premises service under the ordinary rules, engineered work stays engineered, and no Sharma circuit connects to a trolley ground-return system.

FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.
sections.why_it_exists: A ground return puts traction current in the earth and in every buried metal path it can find. Tie a building system into that and you import stray current, shock exposure, and electrolytic corrosion of piping and conductors. The rule keeps two incompatible systems apart, and the exception stays inside buildings the railway itself operates, where the railway's own engineering controls both sides.

sections.exam_trap: The trap answer is that the connection is fine if the voltages match. 110.19 is not a voltage rule. It bans the connection to a ground-return trolley system outright, and the only exception is inside the railway's own car houses, power houses, and stations — not in any building that happens to stand near tracks.

sections.title: Reconditioned equipment
sections.plain_explanation:
This section is new in the 2023 NEC; under NEC 2020 the only general reconditioned-equipment rule is the marking rule in 110.21(A)(2), plus scattered article rules such as 240.62 and 240.88., governs equipment that has been reconditioned — rebuilt or restored — as distinct from equipment that has merely been serviced or had a failed part replaced with an approved equal. Reconditioned equipment has to be evaluated and accepted under the section's terms, the party that reconditioned it has to be identifiable, and some categories of equipment are restricted or not permitted to be reconditioned at all. A previous listing does not automatically survive an extensive rebuild.

NEC 2023 CHANGE:
• 110.20: New section: reconditioned equipment is allowed unless another rule bans it, and it gets accepted through a listing, a field label, the original maker's instructions, or approval by the authority having jurisdiction. Reconditioned equipment is allowed unless a rule elsewhere in the code prohibits reconditioning that item.
FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.
sections.on_the_job: On commercial renovations, treat refurbished switchboards, panelboards and breakers as a question, not a bargain: who reconditioned it, under what evaluation, and is that category of equipment permitted to be reconditioned? Get the answer before it is set, not at inspection.
sections.florida_note: Not in force on Florida jobs under NEC 2020 (permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026). FBC 9th Ed. (NEC 2023) applies to permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026.

nec2023_change.change: New section: reconditioned equipment is allowed unless another rule bans it, and it gets accepted through a listing, a field label, the original maker's instructions, or approval by the authority having jurisdiction. Reconditioned equipment is allowed unless a rule elsewhere in the code prohibits reconditioning that item.

sections.title: Marking — manufacturer marks and field-applied hazard marks
sections.plain_explanation:
Equipment carries the manufacturer's name and its ratings so the user can tell what it is and what it is rated for. Where the Code requires a field-applied hazard marking, it has to be durable enough for its environment, use signal wording everyone recognizes, and not be handwritten where the Code requires a proper marking. A faded or missing rating plate makes equipment hard to approve and harder to service safely. Reconditioned equipment has its own marking rule at 110.21(A)(2): it must be marked with the name or trademark of the business that reconditioned it and the date of reconditioning, identified as reconditioned, and the original listing mark must be removed or voided — reconditioned gear is never passed off as new.

NEC 2023 CHANGE:
• 110.21: Reconditioned gear has to show who rebuilt it, when, and that it's reconditioned. The original listing mark comes off or is made unreadable, but the nameplate can stay. Required: strip off the original listing mark or deface it so nobody can read it. The rest of the nameplate, ratings included, can stay.
FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.
sections.on_the_job: Do not paint over, cover or discard rating labels. When you add a required field marking, use a proper printed label suited to the location, not a marker scrawl.
sections.florida_note: Exterior Florida labels fade fast. Use UV- and moisture-durable labels outside so required markings survive to the next inspection.

nec2023_change.change: Reconditioned gear has to show who rebuilt it, when, and that it's reconditioned. The original listing mark comes off or is made unreadable, but the nameplate can stay. Required: strip off the original listing mark or deface it so nobody can read it. The rest of the nameplate, ratings included, can stay.

sections.title: Identification of disconnecting means
sections.plain_explanation:
Every disconnecting means has to be legibly marked to show what it shuts off, unless the purpose is already obvious from where it sits and what it feeds.
• The exception is narrow: no separate marking is needed only where the purpose is evident from the disconnect's location and arrangement.
• The marking must be durable for its environment. A pencil scrawl that fades in a Florida garage is not durable.
• On a multi-unit or multi-tenant job, each service disconnect and fault-protection device also has to show where its supply side comes from, so no one opens the wrong gear.
sections.on_the_job: Label every breaker and disconnect with its actual load — 'condenser', 'air handler 2', 'water heater' — not 'spare' labels on live circuits or a directory copied from another house. Update the directory whenever a circuit changes. On a four-plex trim-out in Kissimmee, that means a typed or permanent-marker card at punch, each unit's service disconnect marked with the source that feeds it, and the card re-done the same day any circuit moves — not at the next visit.
sections.figure_idea: Panel directory card filled in legibly, one line per breaker, with a crossed-out example directory that just repeats 'lights / receptacles'.

nec2023_change.change: Outside one- and two-family dwellings, a disconnect's label now has to say where its supply source is located, not just which source feeds it. In commercial, industrial and multifamily buildings, each disconnect's label has to identify the panel or source feeding it and where that source sits.

A missing or wrong label means the live circuit stays live while everyone believes it is dead, or the wrong equipment gets killed mid-process. Legible, durable, source-identified marking is what lets a stranger shut the right thing off the first time.

sections.title: Current transformers
sections.plain_explanation:
This section covers current transformers used with electrical equipment, including how unused current transformers mounted in place are to be treated so their secondary circuits are not left in a hazardous state.
• A CT steps a large primary current down to a small secondary current in exact ratio: a CT marked 400:5 delivers 5 A to the meter while the bus carries 400 A.
• The secondary is not an ordinary circuit. It is built to work into a near-short — the meter burden, or a shorting device at a test block.
• Current-transformer secondaries behave unlike ordinary branch-circuit conductors: an open-circuited secondary under load can produce dangerous voltage, which is why the section and the equipment instructions govern their handling.
• An unused CT that stays mounted gets its secondary shorted and made safe — never left open.
sections.on_the_job: Metered 800 A commercial service in Winter Garden: the CTs sit on the bus ahead of the meter. Swapping the meter, the tech shorts every CT secondary at the shorting block before lifting a single lead, and the spare CT mounted for a future tenant gets its secondary shorted and tagged — not left open. On metered commercial services, never open a CT secondary casually and never leave a mounted spare CT with its secondary open: follow the equipment instructions and this section, or hand it to the person who does this work regularly.
sections.edition_note:
No NEC 2023 change found for this page in the public 2023 change sources reviewed.
FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.
sections.why_it_exists: A current transformer stays tame only while its secondary current has somewhere to go. The primary and secondary ampere-turns balance each other; open the secondary and that balance disappears, the core saturates, and the transformer answers by driving the voltage at the open terminals up until something gives — insulation, an arc, or the person holding the leads. It is a metering device that turns into a voltage hazard the moment its loop is broken.
inspection_fails: Spare CT mounted on the bus with its secondary leads coiled up and left open.
Meter pulled while CT secondary leads were lifted and left dangling, still live from the primary.
Shorting link at the CT test block removed during testing and never replaced.
Secondary leads cut during demolition while the service stayed energized.
sections.exam_trap: The trap: 'the meter is off, so the CT secondary is dead.' Wrong. The primary bus is still carrying load, and the open secondary is exactly when a CT produces its dangerous voltage. A CT secondary is quiet only while it is shorted or connected to its burden — never because the meter stopped reading.

sections.title: Available fault current — field marking and documentation
sections.plain_explanation:
110.24 has two parts, and both are about one number — the maximum available fault current at the service:
• 110.24(A) — marking: service equipment in other than dwelling units must be legibly marked in the field with the maximum available fault current and the date the fault-current calculation was performed. The marking must be durable enough for the environment, and the calculation must be documented and made available to those authorized to design, install, inspect, maintain or operate the system.
• 110.24(B) — keep it current: when a modification to the installation changes the available fault current, the calculation is redone, the marking is updated, and the equipment ratings are rechecked.
Dwelling unit service equipment is the exception — it does not have to carry this marking.
sections.on_the_job: On service changes, ask for the fault-current figure, mark it with its date, and check it against the interrupting ratings of the gear you are setting under 110.9. Keep the calculation with the job documents. On a small commercial service upgrade in Ocala, the utility's figures put the available fault current at 22 kA — the same worked example the 110.9 page uses. The crew field-marks the new Siemens service equipment “Available fault current: 22 kA” with the date of the calculation, files the calculation in the job folder, and confirms the breakers are 22 kAIC, not 10 kAIC. The old gear being replaced carried no marking at all — nobody could say what it was rated to interrupt.
sections.figure_idea: Service disconnect with a field marking plate reading available fault current and calculation date, and an arrow to the job folder holding the calculation.
sections.florida_note: Utility transformer upgrades in growing Florida subdivisions are a common reason available fault current rises. Recheck on service upgrades in developed neighborhoods.
sections.why_it_exists: Fault current is invisible, and it only ever goes up. Gear rated below the available fault current can fail violently instead of opening when a hard fault hits — that is the 110.9 problem, and 110.24 is how the next person finds out about it. The dated marking tells an inspector, a maintenance tech, or Sharma on a service upgrade whether the equipment in front of them still matches what the utility can deliver.
sections.exam_trap: Two traps. First: the marking is required on dwelling unit services — it is not; 110.24 applies to service equipment in other than dwelling units. Second: the number is marked once and forgotten — 110.24(B) requires the calculation, the marking and the equipment ratings to be revisited when a change alters the available fault current.

sections.title: Lockable disconnecting means
sections.plain_explanation:
Some rules in this Code do not ask for a disconnect in sight of the equipment. They ask for one that can be locked open instead. Section 110.25 sets what "lockable" has to mean wherever another rule uses that option:
• The disconnect must be capable of being locked in the open position.
• The provision for locking is part of the installation. It is installed with the disconnect and stays in place whether or not a padlock is on it today.
• The person doing the work applies their own lock and keeps control of it while the work goes on.
A breaker fitted with a listed lock-off device that lives on the breaker can meet this. A wrap of wire, a strip of tape, or a zip tie around a handle cannot: none of them is installed as part of the disconnect, and none of them stays in place when the lock comes off. And 110.25 does not create the option by itself — where the governing rule never offered a lockable route, the disconnect still has to be where that rule puts it.
sections.on_the_job: On a Kissimmee service call, the air-handler blower's only disconnect was the breaker in the garage panel, about 70 ft away and out of sight. Article 430 allows that arrangement only where the breaker is capable of being locked open, so we fitted the breaker with a listed lock-off provision that stays mounted on it. The tech now hangs his own padlock before he climbs into the attic, and the provision is still there for the next visit. Wherever you rely on the lockable route instead of an in-sight disconnect, confirm the provision is real, permanent hardware before you trust it.
sections.why_it_exists: Lockout is how a servicer makes sure the equipment in front of them stays dead while their hands are in it. An improvised lock can fall off, be cut, or be ignored, and the circuit comes back with somebody still working on it. A permanent provision that is always there — lock or no lock — makes the safe move the easy move, every visit, for every tech who follows.
sections.exam_trap: The trap answer: "Any disconnect becomes lockable if you carry a padlock and hasp in the truck, so 110.25 is satisfied." No. The provision for locking must be installed and remain in place with or without the lock. The second trap is using 110.25 where the governing rule never offered a lockable option — it defines the word for the rules that do, like 430.102(B) and 440.14; it is not a stand-alone permission to move a disconnect out of sight.

sections.title: Spaces about electrical equipment — the section as a whole
sections.plain_explanation:
Sufficient access and working space must be provided and kept clear around electrical equipment so people can work on it safely and maintain it. The section is five parts that work together:
• (A) Working space — the clear box in front of the equipment: depth from Table 110.26(A)(1); width 30 in or the equipment width; height 6½ ft or the equipment height; doors open at least 90°.
• (B) Clear space — the working space is not storage space. It stays empty for the life of the installation, not just on inspection day.
• (C) Entrance and egress — at least one way in and out. Equipment rated 1200 A or more and over 6 ft wide needs an entrance at each end; personnel doors near it open in the direction of egress with listed panic hardware.
• (D) Illumination — light for the working space, and it may not be controlled by automatic means only.
• (E) Dedicated equipment space — the equipment's own footprint, from the floor to 6 ft above the equipment or to the structural ceiling, indoors and outdoors. Foreign pipes and ducts stay out of it.
Space that exists on rough-in day and is filled by the plumber's water heater later is not working space. Each part has its own page; this page is the map.
sections.on_the_job: Defend the space from rough-in to final. On a Marion Oaks garage panel we tape the box on the slab at rough-in: 30 in wide, 3 ft out from the cover, floor to 6½ ft, plus the dedicated space above it running 6 ft over the panel. The builder's shelving and the plumber's water heater get drawn outside those lines before either trade sets anything. Coordinate early — once a water heater or shelving unit is set inside the panel's space, somebody is moving something, and it is cheaper if it is not us at final.
sections.sharma_note: S-09 back-to-back meter and panel is Sharma's preferred layout, and it still owes this section its full working space in front of the panel.

nec2023_change.change: Open doors on any equipment can't shrink the exit path below 24 inches by 6½ feet, working-space floors have to be flat as practical, and dedicated space now includes service equipment. Doors on any equipment, opened at once, can't leave less than 24 inches of width or 6½ feet of height to get in or out.
nec2023_change.source: Electrical Exam Coach, 2023 NEC change summary: 110.26 Working space and egress

sections.why_it_exists: Every part of 110.26 protects the same moment: a person working on live equipment who needs room to stand, light to see by, and a way out. Gear gets serviced for decades after we leave. If the space is gone, the next worker crowds the panel, works in the dark, or has no escape when something flashes.
sections.exam_trap: The trap is treating 110.26 as one number — "3 ft in front of the panel." The depth is only part (A). A job can have its 3 ft and still fail: shelves in the clear space, a motion-sensor-only light, a duct through the dedicated space. Run backwards: at 0–150 V to ground the depth is 3 ft in all three conditions; the 3½ ft and 4 ft depths start at 151 V to ground.

sections.title: Working space about equipment
sections.plain_explanation:
Electrical equipment that may need examination, adjustment, servicing or maintenance while energized must have a clear working space in front of it. Picture an invisible box standing on the floor in front of the panel:
• Depth: from Table 110.26(A)(1), measured from the exposed live parts, or from the enclosure front when the parts are enclosed. At 0–150 V to ground (every 120/240 V house panel) it is 3 ft in all three conditions.
• Width: 30 in or the width of the equipment, whichever is greater. The panel does not have to be centered in it.
• Height: floor to 6½ ft, or the height of the equipment, whichever is greater.
Doors and hinged panels must be able to open at least 90° inside that box. Above and below the panel, 110.26(E) adds the dedicated space: the panel's own width and depth, from the floor to 6 ft above the equipment or to the structural ceiling, whichever is lower. Pipes, ducts and other equipment foreign to the electrical installation stay out of it.
sections.on_the_job: Garage panel on a new slab home in Marion Oaks: the plumber wants the water heater beside the panel and the builder wants shelves on that wall. Tape it out at rough-in: 30 in wide wherever the panel sits, 3 ft out from the panel cover, floor to 6½ ft. The water heater goes outside that box and not under the panel, because the dedicated space runs from the floor up. On a small commercial job, a 480Y/277 V panelboard facing a concrete block wall is 277 V to ground and Condition 2, so the depth is 3½ ft, not 3 ft.
sections.sharma_note: S-09 prefers the meter outside and the panel inside, back to back, where the house allows. That layout still has to leave the 110.26 working space in front of the panel.

sections.title: Depth of working space and the three conditions
sections.plain_explanation:
Depth is read from the table in this section, which sets the distance by the voltage to ground and by what faces the worker. Condition 1 is exposed live parts on one side of the space with no live or grounded parts on the other side. Condition 2 puts a grounded surface, such as a concrete or masonry wall, on the far side. Condition 3 puts exposed live parts on both sides. At 0 to 150 volts to ground the table gives 3 ft for all three conditions; the conditions only change the depth at higher voltages — at 151 to 600 volts to ground the depths are 3 ft, 3 ft 6 in, and 4 ft. The worse the exposure across the aisle, the deeper the space must be once voltage makes the conditions diverge.

Table 110.26(A)(1) — minimum depth of working space, by voltage to ground:
• 0–150 V to ground — Condition 1: 3 ft · Condition 2: 3 ft · Condition 3: 3 ft
• 151–600 V to ground — Condition 1: 3 ft · Condition 2: 3½ ft · Condition 3: 4 ft
• 601–1000 V to ground — Condition 1: 3 ft · Condition 2: 4 ft · Condition 3: 5 ft
sections.on_the_job: For a house panel on a wood-framed wall with nothing live across the aisle, Condition 1 and its 3 ft depth for up to 150V to ground is the everyday case. A second panel facing the first makes it Condition 3 — still 3 ft at house voltage, because at 150V or less to ground all three conditions are 3 ft. Recheck the table when the voltage to ground goes above 150V.
sections.figure_idea: Three aisle cross-sections labelled Condition 1, 2 and 3, showing what is on the far wall in each and an arrow pointing to the table for the depth.

sections.title: Width of working space
sections.plain_explanation:
The working space in front of electrical equipment must be at least 30 in. wide, or the width of the equipment itself, whichever is greater. The width is measured so the worker can stand squarely in front of the gear: the space may be arranged with the equipment offset within it, but the 30 in. minimum — or the full equipment width on wider gear — has to be there, and like all working space it must stay clear, not become storage.
• Width: 30 in. minimum, or the width of the equipment if the equipment is wider
sections.on_the_job: A residential panel is usually narrower than 30 in., so the 30 in. rule is the one that governs — measure it before closets, shelving or a water heater get framed into that strip. On wide commercial switchgear, the equipment's own width takes over.
sections.figure_idea: A panel front-on with a 30 in. dimension line across the working space and a wider switchboard beside it measured at its own width.

sections.title: Height of working space
sections.plain_explanation:
The working space must extend from the floor or platform up to a height of 6½ ft, or the height of the equipment itself, whichever is greater. Two everyday exceptions temper the number: in existing buildings, smaller service equipment or panelboards (200A or less, in dwelling-related installations) that do not meet the height may be permitted where the AHJ allows, and meters and meter sockets may project into the space within limits. Equipment above the space — a sprinkler pipe or a duct that is not electrical — is a dedicated-space question under 110.26(E), not a reason to shrink the height.
• Height: 6½ ft minimum, or the height of the equipment if the equipment is taller
sections.on_the_job: Six and a half feet is taller than most helpers pace it off — a standard door header sits right at the line. Check the height before a soffit or duct gets framed over a panel location, and the existing-dwelling exception applies only to existing dwelling units, never to new construction., not assumptions.
sections.figure_idea: A panel elevation with a 6½ ft dimension line from floor to the top of the working space and a duct drawn above the line.

sections.title: Limited access — working space above ceilings and in crawl spaces
sections.plain_explanation: Where equipment of 1000V or less that is likely to need examination, adjustment, servicing or maintenance while energized has to sit in a limited-access space (above a lay-in ceiling, in a crawl space), all of these apply. (a) Above a lay-in ceiling, the opening must be at least 22 in. x 22 in. In a crawl space, the accessible opening must be at least 22 in. x 30 in. (b) The working space width is the equipment width or 30 in., whichever is greater. (c) Enclosure doors and hinged panels must open at least 90 degrees. (d) The depth in front must meet Table 110.26(A)(1). The maximum height is whatever is needed to install the equipment, and a horizontal ceiling structural member or access panel is permitted in the space. NEC 2023 retains this rule; its paragraph number there is to be confirmed against the printed 2023 book.
sections.on_the_job: Air handler disconnects and RTU or attic equipment above T-bar: plan the 22x22 tile and the 90-degree door swing before rough-in.

sections.title: Clear space, entrance and egress, and illumination
sections.plain_explanation: Working space cannot be used for storage. Entrances must let a worker get in and out without squeezing past live parts, and on large equipment (110.26(C)(2)) a second entrance/exit path is required once the service disconnects total 1,200A or more. Personnel doors within 25 ft of the working space have their own rule at 110.26(C)(3): the door must open in the direction of egress and carry listed panic hardware or fire-exit hardware. Working spaces also have to be illuminated so the work is not done by flashlight, and the lighting must not be controlled by automatic means only (110.26(D)) — automatic control may supplement a switch, but it cannot be the only control.
sections.on_the_job: If the panel room doubles as storage, clear it before calling inspection. Check the light over the panel works, and flag any plumbing run directly above electrical gear — that conversation is much easier at rough-in than after a leak.

sections.title: Entrance to and exit from working space
sections.plain_explanation: There must be at least one entrance to and exit from the working space, sized and arranged so a worker can get in, work, and get out without squeezing past the equipment. For large equipment — rated 1200A or more and over 6 ft wide, containing overcurrent, switching or control devices — there must be one entrance to and egress from the working space at each end, at least 24 in. wide and 6½ ft high; a single entrance is permitted where the egress is unobstructed, or where the working space depth is doubled per Table 110.26(A)(1). Doors serving these spaces that open into the working-space area are part of the rule's concern: personnel doors where equipment rated 800A or more containing overcurrent, switching or control devices is installed, personnel doors intended for entrance to and egress from the working space that are less than 25 ft from the nearest edge of the working space must open in the direction of egress and have listed panic hardware. of the equipment must open in the direction of exit travel and be fitted with listed panic hardware, so a worker reacting to an arc event pushes out instead of pulling a door against the blast.
sections.on_the_job: Houses rarely trip the 1200A rule, but the one-entrance principle applies everywhere: never let a panel room get framed so the only way out is past the gear. On commercial jobs with big switchboards, count the entrances at layout, and check the door swing and panic hardware before the doors are hung.
sections.figure_idea: A switchboard room plan: a wide lineup with a door at each end of the working space, arrows showing exit travel away from the gear.

sections.title: Illumination
sections.plain_explanation: Illumination must be provided for the working spaces about service equipment, switchboards, switchgear, panelboards and motor control centers — a worker reading a directory, a torque spec or a fault label cannot be expected to do it in the dark. The light may not be controlled by automatic means only, so a motion-sensor-only setup that can strand a worker in darkness mid-task does not satisfy the rule; there has to be a manual way to keep the light on. No additional lighting outlet is required where the working space is lit by an adjacent light source, or as permitted by 210.70(A)(1) Exception No. 1 for switched receptacles.
sections.on_the_job: A panel in a garage an indoor panel (garage, closet, utility room) needs its light; 110.26(D) does not require a light at an outdoor disconnect.. If the only light on the plan is a motion sensor, flag it at rough-in — adding the manual control after trim is a return trip.

sections.title: Dedicated equipment space
sections.plain_explanation: The floor space equal to the footprint of indoor electrical equipment, from the floor up to 6 ft above the equipment or the ceiling if lower, is dedicated to the electrical installation. Foreign pipes, ducts and other systems cannot pass through that zone except where the section allows, and suspended ceilings with removable panels do not count as the structural ceiling for this purpose. Outdoor equipment has a matching dedicated zone with its own clearances. Foreign systems installed ABOVE that dedicated zone are handled at 110.26(E)(1)(b): they need protection against leaks and condensation so nothing drips onto the electrical equipment below.
sections.on_the_job: This is the rule behind 'the plumber cannot run that line over the panel.' The dedicated zone is the panel's width and depth projected upward. Existing v1 item L-042 covers this space in detail.
sections.figure_idea: A panel with a transparent box drawn above it to the ceiling marked dedicated space — no foreign piping, with a duct rerouted around it.

sections.title: Locked electrical equipment rooms or enclosures
sections.plain_explanation:
110.26(F) is one sentence at the head of the working-space rules: electrical equipment rooms or enclosures housing electrical apparatus that are controlled by a lock are considered accessible to qualified persons.
• 'Accessible' is the Article 100 idea — the equipment can be approached and reached. The lock does not make the gear 'not accessible' to the people the Code counts.
• It is accessible to qualified persons — the people trained for that equipment — not to everyone. The lock is what keeps it that way.
• The sentence settles access only. It changes nothing else in 110.26: the working space in front of the gear, the clear space, and the dedicated space all still apply inside the locked room, exactly as they would in an open one.
sections.on_the_job: A small strip plaza on Silver Springs Boulevard in Ocala: the service room holds a 400 A switchboard and two panelboards, and the landlord keeps the door locked, with keys held by the property manager and by Sharma's foreman. That lock is fine — the room counts as accessible to qualified persons. What failed the walk-through was inside the room: paint cans and a ladder stored in front of the switchboard. The lock never waived the working space; the room has to be kept clear like any other gear location, and the key has to actually reach a qualified person when a breaker trips at night.
sections.unverified_reason: New page written 2026-11-25 from Mike Holt's recheck draft (ruling 3). Verified=false until checked against the printed NEC 2020.
sections.why_it_exists: Live gear has to be reachable by the people qualified to work it, and unreachable by everyone else. Without this sentence, a locked door could be argued both ways — an owner claiming the gear is 'not accessible,' so working space does not apply, or an inspector treating a locked room itself as an access violation. The rule closes both arguments: lock the room, control the keys, and the qualified crew is deemed to have access.
inspection_fails: Locked electrical room used for storage — paint, ladders and spare material stacked in the working space in front of the gear.
The only key held off-site by the owner, so no qualified person on the job can actually get in — access that exists only on paper.
Key handed to unqualified staff to 'go reset the breaker' — accessible to qualified persons is not accessible to everyone.
Gear roughed in with no working space because 'the room will be locked anyway.'
sections.exam_trap: The room is locked, so the equipment is not accessible and no working space is required? Wrong on both ends. 110.26(F) deems the locked room accessible to qualified persons, and the working-space rules apply in full inside it — the lock controls who gets in, it does not shrink the space.

sections.title: Guarding of live parts
sections.plain_explanation:
Live parts of electrical equipment operating at 50 volts or more must be guarded against accidental contact. The usual way is an approved enclosure — covers and deadfronts in place. Where that is not the method, 110.27(A) allows guarding by one of these means instead:
• Location in a room, vault or similar enclosure that only qualified persons can enter
• Permanent, substantial partitions or screens, arranged so only qualified persons can get within reach of the live parts
• Location on a balcony, gallery or platform raised and arranged to shut out unqualified persons
• Elevation above the floor or working surface: at least 8 ft for 50 to 300 volts, at least 8½ ft for 301 to 600 volts
Entrances to rooms and guarded locations holding exposed live parts get conspicuous warning signs. Separately, 110.27(B): where equipment is likely to be exposed to physical damage, its enclosures and guards must be arranged and strong enough to prevent that damage.
sections.on_the_job: Replace every cover you remove, the same day. An open panel with live bus exposed in an occupied building is a guarding failure even if it was only meant to be open for an hour. On a Sharma commercial job, a 120/240 V panelboard in a locked electrical room is guarded two ways at once — enclosure plus a room only qualified people enter. What fails in the field is the in-between case: cover off 'for troubleshooting,' door propped open, storage creeping into the room. Guarding by location only works while the location stays controlled.
sections.why_it_exists: The person who eventually touches an exposed bus is rarely an electrician — it is a homeowner resetting a breaker in the dark, a cleaner, a kid, a tenant's handyman. Guarding assumes an unqualified person will end up in front of the gear sooner or later, and makes sure there is nothing for them to touch.
inspection_fails: Panel cover or deadfront removed and left off in an occupied space — live bus exposed to anyone who walks up.
Electrical room door propped open and the room used for storage — guarding by location fails the moment anyone can wander in.
No warning sign at the entrance to a room where live parts are guarded by location.
Open live parts at reach height 'because only electricians go back there' — no enclosure, no lock, no partitions, no elevation.
sections.exam_trap: The trap is the threshold: many pick 480 V, or 'only where the public can reach it.' The rule starts at 50 volts — 120 V branch circuits and 277 V lighting parts are live parts too, and a locked room full of stored paint is not guarding by location anymore.

sections.title: Enclosure types
sections.plain_explanation:
Enclosures are selected by type for the environment they will live in, and this section's table matches enclosure types to the exposures they are built to withstand — indoor dust and dripping liquid, outdoor rain and sleet, hose-directed water, corrosion, and the like. The common field types run from a general indoor enclosure, through the outdoor rain-tight type crews see on house disconnects, to the corrosion-resistant types used in washdown and coastal work. The type marked on the enclosure, not its appearance, is what it is rated for.

The types Sharma meets most, from the section's table:
• Type 1 — indoor, general purpose; contact and falling-dirt protection
• Type 3R — outdoor; rainproof and sleet-resistant — the standard house disconnect and meter enclosure type
• Type 4 — watertight, including against hose-directed water
• Type 4X — Type 4 performance plus corrosion resistance — washdown and coastal work
• Type 12 — indoor industrial; dust, lint, and dripping noncorrosive liquids
A higher-duty type may substitute for a lower one in many cases, but the marked type is the rating — never the paint or the shape.
sections.on_the_job: Match the type to the real exposure: indoor-type equipment does not go on an exterior Florida wall, and a corroded or wrong-type enclosure found on a service call is a replacement item, not a paint job.
sections.florida_note: Salt air makes enclosure type a live issue on Florida coastal work; corrosion-resistant types earn their cost outdoors near the coast.

sections.title: Equipment over 1000 volts — enclosure and access (overview)
sections.plain_explanation:
110.31 opens Part III of Article 110 — the added rules for installations over 1000 volts, nominal — with how the equipment is enclosed and how access to it is controlled.
• The starting idea: an installation in a vault, room or closet, or in an area surrounded by a wall, screen or fence, with access controlled by a lock or other approved means, is considered to be accessible to qualified persons only. The enclosure is designed and constructed for the nature and degree of the hazard.
• Indoors (110.31(B)): where the installation is accessible to unqualified persons, it is made with metal-enclosed equipment, and switchgear, transformers and similar equipment are marked with appropriate caution signs.
• Outdoors (110.31(C)): a wall, screen or fence encloses the installation to deter access by unqualified persons. A fence is not less than 7 ft high, or a combination of 6 ft or more of fence fabric and a 1 ft or more barbed-wire extension. The distance from the fence to live parts is not less than Table 110.31 gives.
• Vaults (110.31(A)) and enclosed equipment accessible to unqualified persons (110.31(D)) carry added rules of their own inside the section.
Sharma rarely installs this class of work, so this page is an orientation marker rather than a working guide.
sections.on_the_job: If a commercial job crosses into over-1000V equipment, stop and escalate — design, guarding and access rules change materially, and this work is engineered and permitted differently from ordinary premises wiring. Sharma's field work on such a job is limited to what the engineered documents direct, inside the enclosures and access controls the design establishes — not field judgment.

sections.title: Working space, entrances and guarding over 1000 volts (110.32–110.34)
sections.plain_explanation:
Part III continues with the working-space rules for over-1000V equipment — the same concerns as 110.26, in a class of work where the consequences are far worse.
• 110.32 sets the working space about the equipment.
• 110.33 covers entrances to and exits from the working space, including entrance size and panic hardware.
• 110.34 covers the depth of working space (Table 110.34(A) by reference), guarding of live parts, and illumination.
The depths and dimensions live in the printed tables and the design documents — this page is the map, not the numbers. No value from these three sections is published here: until the page is checked against the printed NEC 2020, every dimension waits in print.
sections.on_the_job: Sharma does not design over-1000V work. If a job touches it, the working-space, entrance and guarding questions go to the engineer of record with the printed Part III in hand — stop and escalate. In the field, Sharma's part is to protect what the design establishes: keep the working space clear, keep the entrances unblocked, and report damaged guarding instead of working around it.
sections.sharma_note: Engineered work — escalate. Sharma does not design over-1000V installations.

FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.
sections.why_it_exists: At these voltages the working space is escape space: room to stand square, room to step back, and a door that opens under pressure when a worker is backing away from trouble. Entrances, guarding and illumination sit in the same group of sections because a perfect clearance is worthless if the worker cannot reach it, cannot leave it, or cannot see in it.
inspection_fails: Working space in front of medium-voltage gear used as storage — clear on the drawings, filled in the building.
Entrance to the working space blocked, or door hardware replaced so the door no longer opens under simple pressure.
Guarding over live parts removed for maintenance and never reinstalled.
Working-space illumination out — the gear stands in the dark and the first check is made with a phone light.
sections.exam_trap: The trap is answering an over-1000V working-space question from Table 110.26(A)(1) — the familiar 3 ft house-panel depth. Part III has its own sections and its own table (110.34 and Table 110.34(A)). And on this page the values are deliberately not printed: the correct habit is to check the printed Part III, not to quote a number remembered from premises wiring.

sections.title: Circuit conductors, temperature limits and pre-energization tests over 1000 volts (110.36, 110.40, 110.41)
sections.plain_explanation:
The rest of Part III closes the over-1000-volt installation:
• 110.36 covers the circuit conductors of these installations.
• 110.40 sets the temperature limits at their terminations.
• 110.41 requires inspections and tests before the equipment is energized and put in service.
All three are engineered-work territory: conductor selection, termination temperature and acceptance testing on this class of gear follow the design documents and the printed Code, not field judgment. This page publishes no values from any of the three sections — it has not been checked against the printed NEC 2020, and until it is, the numbers stay in print and in the engineer's documents, where they belong.
sections.on_the_job: If Sharma is asked to connect or energize over-1000V equipment, the inspections and tests of 110.41 are scheduled and documented before energization — and the design questions go to the engineer, not the field. Until those documents exist and the tests are done, the gear stays de-energized.
sections.sharma_note: Engineered work — escalate. Sharma does not design over-1000V installations.
sections.unverified_reason: New orientation page written 2026-11-25 per Mike Holt ruling 4. No table values published. Verified=false until checked against the printed NEC 2020.

sections.why_it_exists: Above 1000 volts, a wrong conductor, an overheated termination or an untested circuit does not end with a tripped breaker and a scorch mark — it can destroy switchgear and kill. The inspections and tests of 110.41 exist so that the first energization is a confirmation of work already proven, not the moment a hidden defect introduces itself.
inspection_fails: Over-1000V equipment energized with no documented pre-energization inspections or tests (110.41).
Conductor or termination decisions made in the field that the design documents never made — engineered work treated as field judgment.
Terminations landed without the termination temperature limits of the design being checked (110.40).
sections.exam_trap: The trap is treating this page as a working guide, or answering a medium-voltage question from house-wiring habit. In this book these three sections are orientation only: their values live in the design documents and the printed Code, and Sharma escalates the design questions to the engineer.
